title: Linux & Shell Basics
summary: Essential Linux commands and shell navigation for LLM work.

sections.beginner:
What: Linux is the OS behind virtually every LLM training run and GPU server. You need ~20 commands: ls/cd/cp/mv/rm, grep, pipes, ssh, tmux, and reading logs.

Why: Training jobs run for hours on remote machines. If you cannot inspect a runaway process or find an error in a 2 GB log, you cannot debug training.

Example: nvidia-smi -l 1 watches GPU memory live; tail -f train.log | grep -i 'loss\|error' follows a run.

Common mistake: running long jobs in a bare SSH session that dies and kills the run — use tmux or a scheduler.
sections.intermediate:
How: manage processes (ps/kill/htop), permissions, environment variables, pip/conda envs, and rsync for moving datasets and checkpoints.

Rule: never train in a laptop session — SSH to the GPU host, start tmux, activate the env, launch with nohup or torchrun, log everything to a file.

Example: torchrun --nproc_per_node=4 train.py 2>&1 | tee run.log keeps output visible and saved.

Trade-off: convenience (notebooks) vs reproducibility (scripts + pinned envs). Scripts win for anything longer than an hour.
sections.advanced:
Implementation: systemd units or Slurm/SGE for scheduling, cgroups for memory limits, disk quotas for checkpoint dirs, SSH multiplexing for multi-node runs.

Failure modes: disk full from checkpoints kills a 3-day run; OOM-killer silently murders the data-loader; stale NFS handles corrupt saves. Monitor all three.

Measure: df -h before launching; alert when checkpoint dir growth rate × remaining steps exceeds free space.
sections.deepdive:
Mechanics: NVIDIA drivers expose GPUs via kernel modules and /dev/nvidia*; containers need the NVIDIA container toolkit to pass them through. Driver ↔ CUDA ↔ PyTorch versions must be mutually compatible (nvidia-smi shows max supported CUDA).

Implication: most 'GPU not detected' failures are version skew, not broken hardware — pin the trio per machine.

title: Python Fundamentals
summary: Python is the primary language of LLM engineering.

sections.beginner:
What: Python is the language of LLM engineering — every framework (PyTorch, Hugging Face, vLLM) is driven from it. Master variables, functions, loops, lists/dicts, file I/O, and virtual environments.

Why: you will spend more time writing data pipelines and eval harnesses than model code. Weak Python = slow everything.

Example: streaming a 50 GB JSONL file line-by-line instead of json.load() is the difference between a working pipeline and an OOM crash.

Common mistake: installing packages globally and breaking the system env — always one venv per project.
sections.intermediate:
How: list/dict comprehensions, generators (yield) for streaming data, context managers for files/checkpoints, dataclasses for configs, argparse for run scripts.

Rule: any dataset bigger than RAM must be a generator/iterator, never a list.

Example: def stream_jsonl(p): for line in open(p): yield json.loads(line) processes arbitrarily large corpora in constant memory.

Trade-off: readability vs speed — profile before optimizing; 90% of ML Python slowness is accidental quadratic loops or per-sample tokenizer calls.
sections.advanced:
Implementation: asyncio for concurrent API eval calls, multiprocessing for CPU-bound tokenization, C extensions/Numba only when profiling proves Python is the bottleneck.

Failure modes: GIL contention in threaded data-loaders (use processes), silent slowdowns from unbatched HF tokenizer calls (use tokenizer.batch_encode), pickle failures on lambdas in multiprocessing.
sections.deepdive:
Mechanics: CPython's GIL allows one bytecode thread at a time — threads help I/O-bound work (downloads, API calls) but not compute. Reference counting + cyclic GC means leaked references in long training loops (appending tensors to a list) grow RAM until OOM.

Implication: detach and move diagnostics to CPU/numpy; never accumulate GPU tensors across steps.

title: Git & Version Control
summary: Track changes, collaborate, and manage experiment code.

sections.beginner:
What: Git tracks code changes; GitHub hosts them. For LLM work its real job is experiment reproducibility: which code + config produced which checkpoint.

Why: 'the good run from Tuesday' is worthless if you cannot reproduce it. Commit code, tag releases, record the commit hash with every run.

Example: write the current git rev-parse --short HEAD into every training log and checkpoint card.

Common mistake: versioning datasets or checkpoints in Git — use DVC/S3 + a version string instead.
sections.intermediate:
How: branches per experiment, git bisect to find which commit broke training, hooks to block commits with secrets, Git LFS only for small assets.

Rule: configs are code — the exact YAML/CLI flags of a run belong in the repo history, not in a shell scrollback.
sections.advanced:
Implementation: rebase workflows for clean history, cherry-picks for hotfixes, signed tags for released checkpoints, CI that runs a smoke training step on every PR.

Failure modes: giant histories from committed data files (shallow-clone pain for every collaborator); merge conflicts in generated files (gitignore them).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: Git stores snapshots as content-addressed objects; corruption usually means disk failure, recoverable via git fsck --lost-found plus remote refs. For long runs, push branches before launching — a dead workstation disk must never take the experiment record with it.

title: NumPy & Arrays
summary: Vectorized computation is the basis of all DL frameworks.

sections.beginner:
What: NumPy provides N-dimensional arrays and vectorized math — the mental model behind every tensor operation in PyTorch.

Why: a Python loop over 1M tokens takes seconds; the NumPy equivalent takes milliseconds. All model math is vectorized.

Example: (a * b).sum(axis=1) computes a million dot products at once. Shapes like (batch, seq, hidden) are the vocabulary of the whole curriculum.

Common mistake: ignoring shapes — print .shape after every transform until it becomes reflex.
sections.intermediate:
How: broadcasting rules (align trailing dims), reshape/transpose/stack/split, boolean masking for filtering, einsum for attention-like contractions.

Rule: if you write a Python loop over batch or sequence dims, you are almost certainly doing it wrong.

Example: softmax over vocab: e = np.exp(x - x.max(-1, keepdims=True)); e / e.sum(-1, keepdims=True) — the keepdims + max-subtraction pattern prevents overflow.
sections.advanced:
Implementation: C vs Fortran memory order (row-major default; transposes are views, not copies, until you force one), strided views vs copies, cache-friendly axis ordering for large matmuls.

Failure modes: accidental copies of GB-scale arrays (watch .copy() vs views); non-contiguous arrays silently slowing downstream torch ops.
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: NumPy dispatches to SIMD/BLAS kernels — the same reason PyTorch matmuls are fast. A PyTorch tensor shares this strided-array model, adding autograd history and device placement. Understanding strides explains why permute is free but the following view may copy.

title: Linear Algebra
summary: Matrices, vectors, and operations that power every neural network.

sections.beginner:
What: vectors, matrices, matmul, transpose, dot products, norms. A transformer is ~95% matrix multiplication plus a few nonlinearities.

Why: every layer maps (batch, seq, in) × (in, out) → (batch, seq, out). If matmul shapes confuse you, nothing downstream will make sense.

Example: a hidden size of 4096 means each token is a 4096-dim vector; a Q-projection is a 4096×4096 matrix (~16.8M params in BF16 ≈ 33.6 MB).

Common mistake: confusing elementwise multiply with matmul — attention scores need the latter.
sections.intermediate:
How: rank (independent directions in a matrix), eigendecomposition/SVD (what a matrix stretches vs squashes), norms as regularizers and clipping thresholds.

Rule: LoRA works because weight updates are empirically low-rank — a 4096×4096 update can be approximated by 4096×16 times 16×4096 (~0.8% of params).

Example: gradient clipping by global norm rescales the update vector when its L2 norm exceeds a threshold — pure linear algebra as a stability tool.
sections.advanced:
Implementation: Kronecker-factored curvature (K-FAC) for second-order insight, tensor decompositions for compression, orthogonal initialization to preserve gradient norms at step 0.

Failure modes: ill-conditioned projections (huge condition number) amplify FP16 rounding error — one more reason BF16 dominates training.
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: matmul error grows with inner dimension and shrinks with wider mantissa — BF16 keeps FP32's 8-bit exponent (range) while FP16's 5-bit exponent overflows on large activations. Mixed precision accumulates in FP32 precisely to bound this error. Condition numbers quantify the worst case: κ(A) = σmax/σmin.

title: Calculus for ML
summary: Derivatives and gradients are how models learn.

sections.beginner:
What: derivatives (how fast a function changes), partial derivatives (change w.r.t. one input), gradients (the vector of all partials). Training = follow the negative gradient downhill.

Why: the gradient answers 'which way should each of 7B weights move to reduce loss'. Everything else is logistics around that question.

Example: loss 2.5 → gradient step → loss 2.48. Repeat a trillion times and you get an LLM.

Common mistake: thinking zero gradient means done — saddle points and plateaus also have ~zero gradients.
sections.intermediate:
How: chain rule applied to layered graphs (each layer multiplies local Jacobians), directional derivatives (what loss does along the update direction), gradient norms as a health metric.

Rule: log gradient norms per step. Healthy training: norms stable within ~1 order of magnitude. Exploding/vanishing norms precede NaN and stagnation.
sections.advanced: Implementation: reverse-mode autodiff (one forward + one backward gives all 7B partials — forward-mode would need 7B passes), Jacobian-vector products for analysis, Hessian spectra for sharpness research.
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: reverse-mode AD applies the chain rule from loss backwards, storing (or recomputing, with checkpointing) intermediates. Symbolic differentiation derives formulas; numerical differentiation approximates them and accumulates error — frameworks use AD, which is exact up to floating-point rounding.

title: Probability & Statistics
summary: Understanding uncertainty, distributions, and evaluation metrics.

sections.beginner:
What: random variables, distributions, expectation, variance, Bayes' rule. A language model outputs a probability distribution over the next token.

Why: temperature, top-p, perplexity, and cross-entropy are all probability concepts. You cannot tune sampling without them.

Example: temperature 0 = always the argmax token (deterministic); temperature 1 = sample the raw distribution; higher = flatter, weirder output.

Common mistake: treating a single greedy sample as 'what the model thinks' — the distribution is the belief; one sample is one draw.
sections.intermediate:
How: maximum likelihood (training = make real text probable), cross-entropy = negative log-prob of the true token, KL divergence = distance between distributions.

Rule: cross-entropy loss 2.0 → perplexity e² ≈ 7.4. Quote both; loss for optimization, perplexity for humans.

Example: label smoothing spreads 10% of target probability mass over all tokens — a probabilistic regularizer against overconfidence.
sections.advanced:
Implementation: confidence intervals for benchmark scores (a 1% MMLU gap on 14k questions is ~±0.5%, often noise), significance tests before claiming a win, calibration (does 80% confidence mean 80% accuracy?).

Failure modes: celebrating benchmark deltas smaller than measurement error; ignoring run-to-run variance from data order and init.
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: entropy H(p) = −Σ p log p measures uncertainty in nats; cross-entropy H(p,q) = H(p) + KL(p‖q) is what training minimizes; perplexity = exp(cross-entropy) converts it back to an interpretable 'effective vocabulary size'. This is why PPL = exp(loss) exactly.

title: Optimization Fundamentals
summary: How gradient descent actually works.

sections.beginner:
What: gradient descent: compute gradient, step weights opposite to it, repeat. The learning rate scales the step.

Why: every optimizer (SGD, Adam, AdamW) is a variation on this loop. LR too big → diverge; too small → never finish.

Example: 7B model, LR 3e-4 with warmup then cosine decay — the most common starting recipe in open LLM training.

Common mistake: tuning the optimizer before the learning rate. LR matters more than optimizer choice.
sections.intermediate:
How: momentum (average past gradients to damp oscillation), Adam (per-parameter adaptive steps from gradient mean + variance), AdamW (decoupled weight decay so regularization doesn't pollute the adaptive rates).

Rule: default to AdamW (β1=0.9, β2=0.95, weight decay 0.1, grad clip 1.0) for pretraining; adjust LR first, betas last.

Trade-off: SGD uses less memory (no m/v buffers) but converges slower on transformers — rarely worth it above 1B params.
sections.advanced:
Implementation: saddle points (not local minima) dominate high-dim landscapes; warmup escapes early sharp regions; LR-batch scaling (double batch ≈ +√2 LR as a starting guess, then verify).

Failure modes: loss spikes from too-aggressive decay restarts; frozen training from LR 10x too small (looks like a data bug).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: convergence rates depend on smoothness (Lipschitz gradients) and noise (gradient variance ∝ 1/batch). Schedules matter more than optimizer flavor because they control the noise-floor vs speed trade-off across the run: large steps early (explore), small steps late (settle). Sharpness-aware methods explicitly penalize sharp minima.

title: Machine Learning Fundamentals
summary: From datasets to models: the ML workflow.

sections.beginner:
What: supervised learning (input→label pairs), splits (train/val/test), overfitting (memorizes train, fails val), and the bias-variance trade-off.

Why: 'train loss down, val loss up' is the single most important diagnostic in all of ML — it means memorization, not learning.

Example: fine-tune on 500 examples for 20 epochs: train loss → 0, real quality collapses. That gap is overfitting, measurable only because you held out validation data.

Common mistake: tuning on the test set until it looks good — that makes it a second validation set (contamination by process).
sections.intermediate:
How: stratified splits, cross-validation for small data, accuracy/precision/recall/F1 for classification-style evals, early stopping on validation loss.

Rule: lock the test set before training starts; touch it only for final reporting. All decisions use validation.

Trade-off: bigger validation = better decisions but less training data. 1–5% is typical at LLM scale.
sections.advanced: Implementation: regularization ladders (dropout → weight decay → data augmentation → early stopping), ensembles for variance reduction, learning-curve analysis to decide data vs capacity vs tuning.
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: classical VC/Rademacher bounds say overparameterized models should fail — yet LLMs generalize. Current explanations invoke implicit regularization (SGD prefers flat minima), double descent, and benign overfitting. Practically: scale + data quality beat theory-guided capacity limits.

title: Overfitting vs Underfitting
summary: Read the train/val gap and know which side you are on.

sections.beginner:
What: overfitting = train loss falls, val loss rises (memorized, not learned). Underfitting = both stuck high (model/data/training too weak to capture the pattern).

Why 'train down, eval worse' happens: capacity + repetition let the model store training specifics (phrasing, noise, labels) that don't transfer. More epochs past the val minimum just engrave the training set.

Example: SFT 5k pairs × 10 epochs: train loss 0.1, held-out quality worse than epoch 2 — textbook overfit; fix: 2 epochs + decay + dropout.
sections.intermediate:
How: diagnose from curves (gap opening = overfit; joint plateau = underfit), then act: overfit → more/better data, fewer epochs, dropout/decay, smaller LR late; underfit → bigger LR, bigger model, longer training, check data bugs first.

Rule: 'more data not always helping' usually means quality/duplication problems (see deduplication) or capacity saturation — plot val vs data scale before buying more tokens.
sections.advanced: Implementation: early stopping on val (patience in steps, not epochs); regularization ladders sized to the gap; double-descent awareness (bigger models can generalize better past the interpolation threshold — don't downsize reflexively).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: bias-variance decomposition frames the trade-off; benign overfitting results show interpolating models generalizing when noise is structured (as in language). Grokking (delayed generalization long after memorization) warns against stopping purely on early val — for algorithmic tasks, extend runs before concluding overfit.

title: Reading Loss Curves
summary: What healthy training looks like — and every unhealthy variant.

sections.beginner:
What: healthy: fast early fall → steady log-linear decline → gentle flattening. Plot smoothed train loss + val loss + LR on shared step axis, log-scale y.

Patterns: flat from step 0 (LR ~10× too small, or frozen graph); instant NaN (LR/precision); sawtooth (too-high LR or poison batches); train↓ val↑ (overfit — stop point was earlier).

Example: loss 11.7 → 3 → 2.2 over the first 5% of steps is normal for 1B+ pretraining; panic only if the slope is wrong, not the absolute value.
sections.intermediate:
How: smooth with EMA (0.9–0.99) but keep raw faintly visible (spikes hide in smoothing); compare against the Chinchilla-predicted band for your N/D; track grad norm + LR alongside loss (norm explosion precedes loss explosion by steps — early warning).

Rule: one anomaly is data; repeating anomalies are config. Skip-and-log single spikes; halt and bisect repeating ones.
sections.advanced: Implementation: spike protocol (skip step, log batch hashes, rollback if val degrades, LR ×0.5 on repeat); plateau triage (LR too low vs data exhausted vs capacity — test with a 10× LR probe on a branch); loss-scale vs downstream correlation checks (falling loss + flat evals = mix/tokenizer issue).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: loss follows power-law-plus-constant in healthy scaling runs; deviations have signatures: step-function drops (data-mixture phase changes), slope breaks (schedule horizon mismatches), variance growth (batch too small for the LR). Fit L = E + A·S^−α on your own curve to forecast run completion and detect silent divergence early.

title: Tensors & Autograd
summary: PyTorch tensors and automatic differentiation.

sections.beginner:
What: tensors are N-dim arrays on CPU or GPU with autograd tracking. torch.tensor, .shape, .to('cuda'), .backward() is 80% of daily use.

Why: device placement bugs (CPU tensor meets GPU model) and shape bugs are the two most common PyTorch crashes.

Example: x = torch.randn(4, 512, 4096, device='cuda'); y = layer(x); loss = y.sum(); loss.backward() — forward, scalar loss, backward.

Common mistake: calling .backward() on a non-scalar without grad weights, or forgetting optimizer.zero_grad() so gradients accumulate silently.
sections.intermediate:
How: computation graphs (ops record history), .detach() to cut tracking, in-place ops (_ suffix) that corrupt saved activations, no_grad() for eval/inference.

Rule: eval and generation always run under torch.no_grad() — otherwise you pay backward-graph memory for zero benefit.

Example: logging loss.item() (Python float) instead of keeping the tensor avoids pinning the whole graph in memory.
sections.advanced:
Implementation: custom autograd.Function (forward + backward definitions) for novel ops, gradient accumulation by summing .grad across micro-batches before optimizer.step(), memory-efficient backward via checkpointing.

Failure modes: in-place ReLU on a checkpointed activation (recompute mismatch); retaining graphs across steps (retain_graph) leaking GBs.
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: PyTorch's engine walks the graph of Function nodes in reverse topological order, calling each backward with upstream grads. Checkpointing replaces stored intermediates with re-run segments — trading ~20–30% compute for large memory cuts. torch.compile fuses the forward graph to cut dispatch overhead.

title: Neural Networks
summary: From perceptrons to modern architectures.

sections.beginner:
What: stacked layers: linear map → nonlinearity → repeat, ending in a prediction. A classifier in PyTorch is ~20 lines: nn.Linear, ReLU, loss, optimizer step.

Why: depth composes simple functions into complex ones — the same pattern scales from MNIST to 70B LLMs (which are just very deep, very wide versions with attention).

Example: nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(784,256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256,10)) — forward pass turns pixels into class scores.

Common mistake: stacking linear layers with no activation — N linear layers collapse to one, no matter how many you add.
sections.intermediate:
How: init schemes (Xavier/Kaiming keep activation variance stable at step 0), pooling/normalization placement, writing a clean train loop (forward → loss → backward → clip → step → zero_grad).

Rule: verify a new architecture by overfitting one batch first — if it cannot memorize 8 samples, the bug is in the model, not the data.
sections.advanced: Implementation: residual connections + pre-norm (the combination that lets 100+ layer nets train), stochastic depth/DropPath as depth-wise regularization, width-vs-depth scaling for a fixed param budget.
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: universal approximation says one wide layer can fit anything — but depth is exponentially more parameter-efficient for compositional functions like language. Depth's price is gradient attenuation, paid with residuals and normalization. Empirically, depth scales reasoning while width scales memorization capacity.

title: Activation Functions
summary: ReLU, GELU, SwiGLU — the non-linearity that makes networks learn.

sections.beginner:
What: nonlinearities applied after linear maps. Without them, deep nets collapse to a single linear function. ReLU (max(0,x)) is the classic; GELU/SiLU dominate modern LLMs.

Why: language is nonlinear — negation, conditionals, and composition cannot be expressed by linear maps alone.

Example: swap ReLU→GELU in a small transformer and training curves smooth out slightly; at 7B+ the gap matters enough that everyone uses gated variants.

Common mistake: sigmoid/tanh in deep stacks — saturating gradients stall training (fine for gates, bad for main path).
sections.intermediate:
How: GELU (smooth ReLU, BERT/GPT heritage), SiLU/Swish (x·sigmoid(x), LLaMA FFNs), SwiGLU (gated: two projections multiplied, one through SiLU).

Rule: match the activation to the architecture family you copied (LLaMA → SwiGLU/RMSNorm/SiLU) — mixing conventions silently changes param counts and behavior.
sections.advanced: Implementation: gated FFNs triple the FFN matmuls (gate, up, down) — budget params accordingly; fused SiLU+multiply kernels recover speed; some inference engines only support specific variants.
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: in FP16, saturating activations (sigmoid/tanh) quantize badly near asymptotes; SiLU/GELU are smoother under quantization. Recomputation-friendly activations (cheap to recompute) are preferred under gradient checkpointing since they get re-executed on the backward pass.

title: Loss Functions
summary: Cross-entropy, contrastive loss, and what loss actually means.

sections.beginner:
What: a single number measuring 'how wrong'. Language models minimize cross-entropy: the negative log-probability of the true next token, averaged over positions.

Why: lower cross-entropy = the model assigns higher probability to real text. Perplexity is just exp(loss) in human-readable units.

Example: loss 2.3 ≈ perplexity 10; loss 1.6 ≈ perplexity 5. A randomly-initialized 7B model starts near ln(vocab) ≈ 11.7 loss.

Common mistake: comparing losses across different tokenizers — per-token loss depends on tokens-per-word, so only same-tokenizer comparisons are valid.
sections.intermediate:
How: label smoothing (distribute ε mass to non-targets), focal loss (down-weight easy tokens), contrastive losses (pull good pairs together), DPO loss (prefer chosen over rejected without RL).

Rule: mask padding and (for SFT) prompt tokens out of the loss — training on padding teaches the model to emit pad tokens.
sections.advanced:
Implementation: DPO reparameterizes the RLHF objective into a classification loss over preference pairs with a β temperature and a reference-model anchor; REINFORCE-style losses need KL penalties to stop reward hacking.

Failure modes: DPO collapse (both chosen and rejected likelihoods fall — watch margins, not just loss); length bias (longer chosen responses teach verbosity).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: minimizing cross-entropy = maximum likelihood = minimizing KL(true‖model) + constant. Perplexity = exp(CE) is the effective branching factor. This identity is why pretraining on next-token prediction is statistically principled, not just a heuristic.

title: Learning Rates & Schedulers
summary: The single most important hyperparameter.

sections.beginner:
What: the step-size multiplier on every gradient update. The most important hyperparameter: a wrong LR ruins runs that everything else got right.

Why: too high → loss explodes/NaN within hundreds of steps; too low → flat curves that look like data bugs but are just slowness.

Example: 7B pretraining commonly peaks around 3e-4; SFT on the same model uses ~1e-5–2e-4 (smaller, to avoid destroying pretrained features).

Common mistake: copying a pretraining LR into fine-tuning — fine-tuning almost always needs a smaller LR plus warmup.
sections.intermediate:
How: LR finder (sweep up until loss diverges, pick ~10× below), one-cycle/cosine schedules, layer-wise decay (lower layers get smaller LRs in fine-tuning).

Rule: when doubling batch size, scale LR by ~√2 (conservative) to ~2× (aggressive) — then verify with a short run, never trust the rule blindly.

Trade-off: large LR trains fast but spikes; small LR is stable but may underfit in a fixed token budget.
sections.advanced:
Implementation: warmup length ~1–3% of steps (lets Adam's variance estimates stabilize), decay to ~10% of peak (not zero — wastes capacity), separate LR for embeddings vs body in continued pretraining.

Failure modes: loss spike mid-run after decay restart; NaN at step ~0 from missing warmup with large batches.
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: stability bounds scale inversely with sharpness (max Hessian eigenvalue) — warmup works because early gradients are noisy and sharp. LLM-specific: attention logits grow with width, so wider models need relatively smaller LRs; μP (maximal update parametrization) formalizes LR transfer across widths so small-model sweeps predict large-model optima.

title: Training Schedulers
summary: How learning rate changes over the training run.

sections.beginner:
What: a schedule changes the LR during training: warm up from ~0, hold/decay, finish low. Cosine-with-warmup is the default that works almost everywhere.

Why: early steps need caution (random weights, noisy Adam stats); late steps need small moves (settle into the minimum). One constant LR cannot do both.

Example: 10k-step SFT: 300-step linear warmup → cosine decay from 2e-4 to 2e-5.

Common mistake: decaying to exactly 0 with restarts on short runs — the restart spike can wipe fine-tuned behavior.
sections.intermediate:
How: linear warmup + cosine decay (pretraining), constant-with-warmup (short SFT), triangular/one-cycle (fast fine-tuning), per-layer schedules (discriminative fine-tuning).

Rule: warmup ≈ 1–3% of total steps; minimum LR ≈ 10% of peak. Set total steps from the token budget first — the schedule needs the horizon.
sections.advanced:
Implementation: step-based (not epoch-based) schedules for token-budgeted runs; resume-safe scheduler state in checkpoints (step count + LR); lookahead/warm-restart variants for exploration.

Failure modes: resumed run resets the schedule (LR jumps back to peak → spike); schedule computed on epochs while data size changed (horizon mismatch).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: theory favors decaying steps as gradient noise dominates late training (∝ 1/t under strong convexity; cosine approximates this while staying high longer). Warmup's role is specific to adaptive optimizers: Adam's second-moment estimates are biased early, and large steps on bad curvature estimates diverge — warmup keeps steps small until estimates settle.

title: Regularization
summary: Preventing overfitting: dropout, weight decay, and more.

sections.beginner:
What: techniques that fight memorization: weight decay (penalize large weights), dropout (randomly zero activations), early stopping (quit when val loss rises).

Why: fine-tuning on 10k examples with a 7B model will memorize them in a few epochs without regularization — train loss 0, real quality worse.

Example: SFT with dropout 0.05–0.1 + weight decay 0.01–0.1 + 2–3 epochs beats 10 unregularized epochs on held-out quality.

Common mistake: heavy dropout in pretraining at scale — with trillions of tokens, the data regularizes itself; dropout just slows training.
sections.intermediate:
How: DropPath/stochastic depth (drop whole residual branches), label smoothing, mixup (blend samples), gradient clipping (cap update norms — stability-flavored regularization).

Rule: regularize hardest where overfitting lives: small SFT sets get dropout + decay + few epochs; massive pretraining gets almost none.
sections.advanced:
Implementation: in AdamW, weight decay is decoupled (subtracted after the adaptive step) — unlike L2-in-loss, which gets mangled by per-parameter scaling. Tune decay in {0.01, 0.05, 0.1} for fine-tuning.

Failure modes: decaying LayerNorm/bias params (usually excluded); decay so high the model underfits (val loss never falls).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: L2-in-loss + Adam adapts the penalty per parameter (scale-inconsistent); AdamW's decoupled form applies true θ ← θ − λθ regardless of gradient scale. At LLM scale, implicit regularization (SGD noise ∝ LR/batch) often dominates explicit terms — another reason batch size and LR are regularization knobs, not just speed knobs.

title: Normalization
summary: LayerNorm, RMSNorm, and why normalization is critical for transformers.

sections.beginner:
What: normalization rescales layer inputs to stable statistics (mean ≈ 0, variance ≈ 1). Transformers use LayerNorm/RMSNorm; BatchNorm belongs to CNNs.

Why: without it, activation magnitudes drift across 32–100 layers until gradients vanish or explode. Every modern LLM normalizes every block.

Example: pre-norm block: x + Attn(Norm(x)) then x + FFN(Norm(x)) — norms on the branch inputs, clean residual highway.

Common mistake: BatchNorm in transformers — batch statistics are unstable for variable-length text; use LayerNorm/RMSNorm.
sections.intermediate:
How: LayerNorm (center + scale), RMSNorm (scale only — cheaper, equally good in practice), pre-norm (stable, standard) vs post-norm (better peak, unstable deep).

Rule: pre-norm + RMSNorm is the safe default for anything you train yourself (LLaMA/Mistral convention).
sections.advanced: Implementation: fused norm kernels; norms kept in FP32 even under AMP (cheap, stabilizes); DeepNorm/Sandwich variants for 100+ layer stability; norm placement interacts with warmup length.
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: RMSNorm drops the mean-centering: x/√(mean(x²)+ε) · g. Centering costs a pass and rarely helps language modeling — hence identical quality at lower cost. Pre-norm keeps the residual stream unscaled (gradient highway); post-norm repeatedly rescales it, which amplifies with depth and demands careful init.

title: Batch Normalization
summary: Stabilizing training by normalizing layer inputs.

sections.beginner:
What: BatchNorm normalizes using per-batch statistics (plus running averages for inference). Dominant in vision CNNs, largely absent from LLMs.

Why it matters here: mainly as a contrast — understanding why it fails for text (variable lengths, tiny per-GPU batches, train/inference statistic mismatch) explains why LayerNorm won transformers.

Common mistake: porting a BatchNorm habit into a transformer codebase.
sections.intermediate:
How: small batches make batch statistics noisy (the classic failure); fused implementations help CNNs; SyncBatchNorm aggregates stats across GPUs at a communication cost.

Rule: if a transformer tutorial contains BatchNorm, treat the whole tutorial with suspicion.
sections.advanced: Implementation: distributed BatchNorm needs cross-GPU stat sync every forward pass — latency-sensitive and brittle under uneven micro-batches. One more reason LLM stacks standardized on per-sample norms.
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: BatchNorm couples samples within a batch (train-time behavior depends on batchmates), breaking the per-sequence independence language modeling assumes and interacting badly with mixed precision (statistic overflow in FP16). LayerNorm/RMSNorm are per-sample: no cross-sample coupling, no sync, no train/inference mismatch.

title: Training Loops
summary: Building a correct training loop from scratch.

sections.beginner:
What: the five-line loop everything rests on: forward → loss → backward → optimizer step → zero grads. Plus a validation pass that never updates weights.

Why: most 'model won't learn' bugs live here (missing zero_grad, stepping without backward, computing val loss with grad enabled), not in the architecture.

Example: opt.zero_grad(); loss = model(batch); loss.backward(); clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0); opt.step()

Common mistake: forgetting eval mode + no_grad during validation — inflated memory and dropout still active.
sections.intermediate:
How: gradient accumulation (N micro-steps per optimizer step = N× effective batch), AMP mixed precision (autocast + scaler for FP16), progress bars with loss/grad-norm/perplexity, validation every K steps (not epochs).

Rule: smoke-test every loop by overfitting one batch to ~0 loss before any real run.
sections.advanced:
Implementation: FP16 needs GradScaler (unscale → clip → step → update); BF16 usually skips scaling; NaN guards that skip the step and log instead of poisoning weights; deterministic data ordering for resumability.

Failure modes: scaler stuck at tiny values (underflow — switch to BF16); accumulation with BatchNorm-like state (not an LLM issue, but shuffle bugs are); val loop accidentally inside autocast changing numbers.
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: exact op order per step: zero grads → forward (AMP) → scale loss → backward → unscale → clip → optimizer step (FP32 master) → copy back to working weights → scaler update → scheduler step. Swapping clip and unscale silently clips scaled gradients (wrong threshold by the scale factor) — the classic AMP bug.

title: Effective Batch Size
summary: The batch size the optimizer actually sees — and why it drives LR, steps, and memory.

sections.beginner:
What: effective batch = per-device batch × gradient-accumulation steps × GPU count (in sequences; × seq length for tokens). It — not the per-GPU number — determines training dynamics.

Why batch size affects training: bigger batches = cleaner gradient estimates (less noise) per step but fewer steps per epoch. Too small = noisy, unstable; too large = sharp minima, wasted compute past the critical batch size.

Example: batch 2 × accum 8 × 4 GPUs × 2048 tokens = 131k tokens/step. A 1B-token run = ~7,600 steps.

Common mistake: reporting 'batch 2' when the effective batch is 64 — nobody can reproduce or advise you from the wrong number.
sections.intermediate:
How: tokens_per_step = B·A·N·S; steps = total_tokens ÷ tokens_per_step. LR scales with batch (double batch → try ×√2 to ×2 LR, then verify). Gradient noise scale ∝ LR ÷ batch governs the exploration/exploitation trade-off.

Rule: fix the effective batch from the token budget and step budget first; then fit it into memory via accumulation/sharding — never let VRAM dictate optimization.

Trade-off: past the critical batch size, doubling batch halves steps but each step costs double — zero wall-clock win, just less noise. Find it by scaling runs, not theory.
sections.advanced:
Implementation: batch-size warmup (ramp batch alongside LR for early stability); token-based (not sample-based) batching for variable lengths; batch/lr joint sweeps on 1% probes before full runs.

Failure modes: changing accumulation mid-run without rescaling the schedule (horizon shifts silently); micro-batch so small that norms/statistics misbehave (rare in LLMs — no BatchNorm — but throughput collapses).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: SGD noise covariance ≈ (1/B)·Fisher-ish; the noise scale g = LR·(N/B − 1)-style relations predict optimal batch from LR and back. Critical batch size B* ≈ gradient-noise / curvature terms — measurable via a few short runs (McCandlish et al.). Practical consequence: LR and batch are one joint knob, tuned together or not at all.

title: Gradient Accumulation
summary: What accumulation actually does — and what it does not.

sections.beginner:
What: run N small micro-batches, sum their gradients, step once. The optimizer sees the same gradient as one big batch (for mean-reduced losses) while activations only ever hold one micro-batch.

What it actually does: trades step time for memory — identical math, smaller peak. It does NOT change convergence vs the same effective batch (up to numerics).

Example: 24 GB card, target batch 64 × 2048: micro-batch 4 × 16 accum steps = batch 64 in ~6 GB activation footprint.

Common mistake: accumulating without dividing (or double-dividing) the loss — verify against a single big-batch step on a probe.
sections.intermediate:
How: zero grads → loop micro-batches (loss ÷ N, backward, no step) → clip → step → zero. With DDP, skip gradient sync on non-step micro-batches (no_sync) to avoid N× communication.

Rule: accumulation changes wall-clock only; keep LR/schedule tied to the effective batch, not the micro-batch.
sections.advanced: Implementation: DDP no_sync + final sync; FSDP reduce-scatter on step boundary; deferred clipping (clip after full accumulation, on unscaled grads); checkpoint-resume must persist the accumulation counter (half-accumulated state is not resumable naively).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: exact equivalence holds for sum/mean reductions with deterministic ops; floating-point summation order differs (error ~1e-7 relative — irrelevant). Communication analysis: DDP without no_sync pays full all-reduce per micro-batch (N× waste); with it, one all-reduce per step. Throughput cost is kernel-efficiency loss on small micro-batches (low occupancy) — size micro-batches to saturate, accumulate for the rest.

title: Gradient Clipping
summary: Cap update norms to survive spikes without slowing normal steps.

sections.beginner:
What: if the global gradient norm exceeds a threshold (usually 1.0), rescale the whole gradient down to it. Normal steps pass through untouched; freak steps get tamed.

Why: one bad batch (corrupt sample, numeric spike) can detonate weights past recovery. Clipping bounds the worst case per step.

Example: torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0) between backward and optimizer step — one line, always on.
sections.intermediate:
How: global-norm clipping (standard) vs value clipping (elementwise, cruder); threshold 0.5–1.0 for pretraining, up to 5 for some fine-tunes; log the norm — chronic clipping (>10% of steps) means LR/batch/data trouble, not a threshold problem.

Rule: clip unscaled grads under AMP (unscale first) — clipping scaled grads applies a threshold off by the scale factor.
sections.advanced: Implementation: per-layer adaptive clipping (AGC — scale-aware, helps large-batch training); interaction with accumulation (clip once per optimizer step, not per micro-batch); FSDP + clipping needs full-grad gathering semantics (use the FSDP-aware clip helper).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: clipping is a trust-region-lite: it bounds the update's Lipschitz impact per step, converting heavy-tailed gradient noise (common in language data) into bounded-variance updates — the convergence proofs for clipped SGD explicitly handle infinite-variance noise that breaks unclipped analysis. It does not fix bias (bad data still pulls); it bounds damage.

title: Checkpoints & Resuming
summary: Saving and restoring training state safely.

sections.beginner:
What: a checkpoint saves everything needed to resume: model weights, optimizer state, scheduler step, RNG states, and data position. Weights alone are not a resumable checkpoint.

Why: a 3-day run that crashes at 90% with only weights saved restarts optimizer statistics from scratch — effectively a different (worse) run.

Example: save every N steps (not epochs): {'model':..., 'optim':..., 'sched':..., 'step':..., 'rng':...} plus the config.

Common mistake: saving only model.state_dict() and calling it a checkpoint.
sections.intermediate:
How: sharded checkpoints for large models (one file per rank), async saving (don't block training on slow disks), keep-last-K + best-val rotation, atomic writes (temp file + rename).

Rule: checkpoint cost = size ÷ disk bandwidth × frequency. Size it so saving costs <2% of runtime.

Trade-off: frequent checkpoints waste I/O; rare ones risk losing days. Hourly + on-plateau is a sane default.
sections.advanced:
Implementation: FSDP/ZeRO-3 needs consolidated-or-sharded save/load with matching world size strategy; CPU offload for optimizer checkpoint assembly; checksums for multi-TB saves; remote upload (S3/GCS) before deleting locals.

Failure modes: loading a sharded checkpoint with a different FSDP version/world size; partial writes from preempted spot instances (atomic rename prevents this); version skew between save and load code.
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: checkpoint I/O is bottlenecked by single-file bandwidth and Python serialization (pickle) overhead — safetensors + sharding fix both (zero-copy, parallel reads). At scale, treat checkpoints as a storage budget: full (weights+optim) every K steps, weights-only snapshots more often, with a manifest mapping steps to files.

title: Tokenization

sections.beginner:
What: tokenizers split text into integer IDs the model eats: 'unhappiness' → ['un', 'happiness']-style pieces. One English word ≈ 1.3 tokens (GPT-style BPE); code/multilingual text costs more.

Why: tokens are the model's real input units — context limits, prices, and dataset sizes are all counted in tokens, not words or bytes. Misunderstanding tokens = misbudgeting everything.

Example: 'Hello, world!' → [9906, 11, 1917, 0] (GPT-2). Same string, different tokenizer → different IDs and different counts.

Common mistake: assuming 1 token ≈ 1 word for budgeting — use the Token calculator; CJK/code can be 2–4× denser in tokens-per-character.
sections.intermediate:
How: BPE (merge frequent pairs — GPT/LLaMA), WordPiece (BERT), Unigram (probabilistic — T5/SentencePiece option). Vocab 32k–128k. Special tokens (BOS/EOS/PAD/UNK) + chat templates wrap turns into the format SFT trained on.

Rule: always use the model's own tokenizer and chat template for fine-tuning and eval — a mismatched template silently degrades instruction following.

Trade-off: bigger vocab compresses text better (fewer tokens/word) but enlarges embeddings + softmax. 128k suits multilingual; 32k suffices for English-centric.
sections.advanced:
Implementation: training SentencePiece/BPE on your corpus (byte-fallback for robustness), adding domain tokens (embedding surgery + brief tuning), pre-tokenization regex (why ' hello' and 'hello' differ), normalization (NFKC) pitfalls for code/math.

Failure modes: tokenizer/model vocab mismatch (logit shape crash); retrained tokenizer with different merge rules on old data (IDs shift silently — re-encode everything).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: BPE is a greedy compression scheme, not linguistically principled — frequent strings get short IDs (efficient), rare strings fragment (long tails, worse modeling). Fertility (tokens/word) varies by language (English ~1.3, some languages 3–8×), which directly scales effective context, cost, and benchmark comparability. Per-token loss comparisons are only valid within one tokenizer — cross-tokenizer, compare bits-per-byte instead.

summary: Splitting text into the token IDs models actually read.

title: Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE)

sections.beginner:
What: Byte-Pair Encoding starts from bytes/characters and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair ('t'+'h' → 'th') until the vocab is full. GPT-2, LLaMA, Qwen tokenizers are BPE variants.

Why: frequent words become single tokens (efficient), rare words compose from pieces (no out-of-vocabulary failures ever — worst case falls back to bytes).

Example: merges learned: 'e'+'r' → 'er', 'th'+'e' → 'the'. 'unbelievable' (rare) → ['un', 'believ', 'able'] while 'the' (common) stays one token.
sections.intermediate:
How: vocab size sets merge count (50k GPT-2, 128k LLaMA-3); pre-tokenizer regex splits text first (numbers, spaces, punctuation get special treatment — GPT's space-aware splits are why leading spaces matter); byte-level BPE handles any Unicode without UNK.

Rule: never strip or normalize text differently at inference than at training — pre-tokenization differences change IDs.
sections.advanced: Implementation: byte-fallback guarantees (every input encodable), special-token handling (added tokens bypass merges — why BOS/EOS stay whole), training your own BPE (sample ≤ tens of GB, dedup first or merges learn spam).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: BPE training is O(corpus × merges) with efficient pair-count updates; encoding is linear with caching. Optimality: greedy merges are not globally optimal compression (Unigram's probabilistic pruning can compress better), but BPE's determinism and simple streaming encode made it the ecosystem winner. Merge-rank artifacts (e.g., ' solid' vs 'solid' as different tokens) are a direct consequence of space-aware pre-splitting.

summary: Merge-based subword tokenization behind GPT and LLaMA.

title: SentencePiece Tokenizer

sections.beginner:
What: SentencePiece is a tokenizer toolkit (Google) that trains directly on raw sentences — no pre-splitting — supporting BPE and Unigram models. T5, PaLM, LLaMA-1/2, Mistral use SentencePiece-trained tokenizers.

Why: language-agnostic (no English-centric splitting rules), reversible (decode(encode(x)) == x exactly, spaces included via ▁ markers), and trainable in one command.

Example: spm_train --input=corpus.txt --model_prefix=tok --vocab_size=32000 --model_type=bpe → tok.model + tok.vocab.
sections.intermediate:
How: Unigram mode starts big and prunes to the best subwords probabilistically (better compression, sampling-based subword regularization possible); BPE mode merges up. Byte-fallback + user-defined symbols for code/special tokens.

Rule: train on a representative sample (deduped, language-balanced) — merges learned on spam stay in your vocab forever.
sections.advanced: Implementation: Hugging Face fast converters preserve the SentencePiece model inside; custom normalizers (NFKC) must match train↔inference; dummy-prefix (leading ▁) handling differs across integrations — verify round-trip on samples.
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: Unigram training runs EM over subword probabilities with Viterbi segmentation, pruning low-loss-reduction pieces — a properly probabilistic objective vs BPE's greedy heuristic. The piece table enables O(n) encoding. Multilingual tension: fixed vocab budget split across scripts raises low-resource fertility — the argument for 128k+ vocabs in multilingual models.

summary: Language-agnostic tokenizer training toolkit (T5, LLaMA, Mistral).

title: Token Embeddings
summary: How words become vectors.

sections.beginner:
What: an embedding table maps each token ID to a dense vector (e.g., 128k vocab × 4096 dims). It is a learned lookup: row i is the model's current representation of token i.

Why: neural nets cannot eat integers — IDs carry no meaning (token 42 vs 43 are unrelated). Embeddings give every token a learnable position in a space where training arranges similar meanings nearby.

Example: after training, king − man + woman ≈ queen emerges in the geometry — not programmed, learned from co-occurrence.

Common mistake: thinking bigger embedding dim is always better — it costs vocab×dim params (128k×4096 ≈ 0.5B params, ~6% of an 8B model).
sections.intermediate:
How: nn.Embedding(vocab, dim); input embed + output head (unprojection to vocab logits). Tied weights share one matrix (saves vocab×dim params); untied keeps two (LLaMA convention, slightly better quality).

Rule: vocab 32k→128k quadruples embedding params — budget it in the Model Calculator, especially for small models where embeddings can exceed 20% of params.

Trade-off: large vocab = fewer tokens per word (shorter sequences, faster training) but a bigger, slower output softmax. 32k–128k is the modern sweet spot.
sections.advanced:
Implementation: soft prompts / prefix tuning freeze the table and prepend learned vectors; embedding surgery (resize + init new rows to mean) when extending vocab for a new language; gradient flows into only the rows present in the batch (sparse update pattern).

Failure modes: resizing embeddings without resizing the output head (shape crash at the logits); new tokens initialized randomly while old ones are trained (new tokens lag for epochs — init from similar tokens instead).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: embedding memory = vocab × dim × bytes (untied: ×2). Lookup is O(1) gather; the output projection is a full matmul over vocab — the reason huge vocabs slow every step. Quantized embeddings (INT8/INT4) are viable for inference since lookups tolerate coarse rows, but keep the output head at higher precision: logit errors directly distort sampling.

title: Attention Mechanism
summary: The core innovation that made transformers possible.

sections.beginner:
What: attention lets each token pull information from other tokens: compare a Query against all Keys, weight the Values by similarity. Q·K → softmax → ×V.

Why: it is the mechanism that resolves 'it' to 'the dog' three sentences back. Without it, fixed-window models cannot do long-range reference.

Example: in 'The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired', the 'it' query attends most strongly to 'animal' — visible in the attention weights.

Common mistake: reading raw attention weights as explanations — heads are noisy and redundant; weights suggest, they don't prove.
sections.intermediate:
How: scaled dot-product: softmax(QKᵀ/√d)V. The √d scale keeps softmax inputs O(1) as dims grow. Causal masks add −∞ above the diagonal; padding masks hide pad tokens.

Rule: attention cost is O(n²·d) time and O(n²) memory for the score matrix — this single fact drives context-length economics (double the context, quadruple attention work).

Example: 8k context, 32 heads: one score matrix per head is 8k×8k = 64M entries ≈ 128 MB in BF16 — times 32 heads ≈ 4 GB per layer without FlashAttention.
sections.advanced:
Implementation: FlashAttention tiles QK/V through SRAM and never materializes the N² matrix (exact, not approximate — same math, O(N) memory); memory-efficient backends (flash, SDPA, xformers) are selected per GPU in modern stacks.

Failure modes: wrong mask dtype/shape silently attends to future tokens (eval looks great, generation is broken); attention dropout left on during eval (nondeterministic scores).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: exact complexity per layer: 4hd² projections + 2n²d attention (forward; ~×3 for backward). Tiling analysis: with SRAM size M, passes ≈ N²d/M — FlashAttention's win is cutting HBM traffic, not FLOPs. Sparse/linear variants (sliding window, Mamba-style SSMs) trade the N² term for N·w or N·d at some quality cost on retrieval-heavy tasks.

title: Self-Attention

sections.beginner:
What: self-attention = a sequence attending to itself (vs cross-attention, which attends to a different sequence, e.g., encoder outputs). Decoder-only LLMs use masked self-attention exclusively.

Why: it builds contextual word meanings: 'bank' gets a different vector in 'river bank' vs 'bank loan' because each occurrence mixes in its neighbors.

Example: layer 0 'bank' ≈ word identity; layer 20 'bank' ≈ word-in-this-sentence (disambiguated by attended context).
sections.intermediate:
How: causal mask (lower-triangular: position i sees ≤ i), padding mask (ignore pads), bidirectional (no mask — encoders like BERT only). KV cache at inference stores past K/V so each new token costs O(n), not O(n²).

Rule: decoder-only generation requires the causal mask in training to match inference — train bidirectional, generate causal, and quality collapses.
sections.advanced: Implementation: mask as additive bias (−inf) vs boolean (backend-dependent numerics — bias form is safer in FP16); sliding-window masks for long context (Mistral); attention sinks (first tokens absorb mass — keep them in cache when evicting).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: causal self-attention is a triangular linear operator per head composed with softmax — during generation it becomes a recurrent update (new K/V appended, one query step). This train-parallel / inference-recurrent duality is exactly what the KV cache exploits: O(n²) total training work becomes O(n) per generated token with O(n) cached state.

summary: How each token attends to every other token in the sequence.

title: Multi-Head Attention (MHA)

sections.beginner:
What: run H attention operations in parallel on H slices of the hidden dim, then concatenate and project. Each head can track a different relation (syntax, coreference, position).

Why: one head must average all relations into a single distribution; 32 heads let relations separate. Empirically, heads specialize (some track syntax, some copy, some are nearly idle).

Example: 4096 hidden ÷ 32 heads = 128 dims per head. Each head's QKᵀ is computed independently, then outputs join through the O-projection.
sections.intermediate:
How: heads = hidden ÷ head_dim (head_dim 64–128 typical). More heads at fixed width = thinner heads (weaker each); head count scales with width in practice (7B: 32 heads; 70B: 64).

Rule: keep head_dim ∈ {64, 128} — Tensor Core kernels are tuned for these; odd head dims waste throughput.
sections.advanced:
Implementation: MQA (1 KV head shared by all queries) and GQA (G query heads per KV head) cut KV-cache memory by heads÷kv_heads (8× for 32→4) at small quality cost — the standard inference optimization in LLaMA-2/3, Mistral, Qwen.

Failure modes: converting MHA→GQA post-hoc by mean-pooling KV heads works (up-training a few B tokens recovers quality) but naive truncation breaks generation.
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: KV-cache bytes per token = 2 (K+V) × layers × kv_heads × head_dim × bytes. For LLaMA-3-8B BF16: 2×32×8×128×2 = 131 KB/token — 8k context ≈ 1 GB per request. GQA's savings are exactly kv_heads/heads; MQA is the limit (kv_heads=1). Benchmarks show GQA-8 within noise of MHA on most suites while serving ~2–3× more concurrent requests.

summary: Parallel attention heads learning different relationships.

title: Multi-Query Attention (MQA)

sections.beginner:
What: Multi-Query Attention shares ONE key head and ONE value head across all query heads. KV cache shrinks by ~heads× (e.g., 32× smaller).

Why: inference memory is dominated by KV cache at long context. MQA trades a little quality for dramatically cheaper, faster serving — the Falcon/PaLM-era answer to serving cost.

Example: 32 query heads + 1 KV head: per-token cache = 2×layers×1×head_dim×bytes instead of ×32.

Common mistake: using MQA for a training-focused build — GQA now dominates because it keeps most of the savings with less quality loss.
sections.intermediate:
How: single K/V projection per layer (hidden → head_dim), broadcast across query heads in the score computation. Trainable params drop slightly (smaller K/V matrices).

Rule: choose MQA only when serving memory dominates everything (very long context, huge batch). Otherwise GQA with 4–8 KV heads.

Trade-off: quality gap vs MHA is small but real on reasoning-heavy evals; capacity bottleneck concentrates in one KV head.
sections.advanced: Implementation: fully compatible with FlashAttention and paged KV managers; up-training MHA→MQA checkpoints needs more tokens than MHA→GQA to recover (fewer KV params to absorb the change).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: MQA is GQA with group size = heads. Theoretical view: KV heads form an information bottleneck of rank kv_heads×head_dim per layer — MQA's rank-1 (per dim-slice) bottleneck is where the quality ceiling comes from. Empirical comparisons show the MHA→GQA-8 gap ≈ noise while MHA→MQA is measurable on hard reasoning sets.

summary: One shared KV head for all queries: maximal inference savings.

title: Grouped-Query Attention (GQA)

sections.beginner:
What: Grouped-Query Attention: groups of query heads share one KV head. GQA-8 on a 32-head model = 8 KV heads = 4× smaller KV cache than MHA, near-identical quality.

Why: the practical sweet spot the whole industry converged on — LLaMA-2/3, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma all ship GQA. You get most of MQA's serving win with almost none of its quality cost.

Example: LLaMA-3-8B: 32 Q heads, 8 KV heads → per-token cache 131 KB BF16; MHA would be 524 KB.
sections.intermediate:
How: pick KV heads ∈ {4, 8} (fewer for serving-optimized, more for quality-optimized); KV projections are hidden → kv_heads×head_dim. Use the Inference Memory calculator to see the batch×context savings for your config.

Rule: 8 KV heads is the default answer; 4 when serving long contexts on tight VRAM; 1 (MQA) only under extreme memory pressure.
sections.advanced:
Implementation: production configs: LLaMA-3-8B (32/8), Mistral-7B (32/8), Qwen-2.5-7B (28/4). Converting checkpoints MHA→GQA by head-pooling + short up-training is established practice.

Failure modes: kv_heads that don't divide cleanly into the tensor-parallel degree (TP splits heads — keep kv_heads divisible by TP size).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: cache per token = 2·L·kv_heads·head_dim·bytes — linear in kv_heads, which is why 32→8 is exactly 4×. Under continuous batching, aggregate KV bytes across the running batch set the max batch size; GQA-8 vs MHA is the difference between serving ~4× concurrent long-context requests on the same GPU. Group-size ablations show diminishing quality returns past 8 KV heads for 7–70B scales.

summary: Grouped KV sharing: near-MHA quality at a fraction of cache.

title: Positional Encoding
summary: Giving the model a sense of token order.

sections.beginner:
What: attention is order-blind — shuffle the tokens and it computes the same thing. Positional encodings inject order so 'dog bites man' differs from 'man bites dog'.

Why: without position info the model is a bag of words. Every LLM capability involving sequence (grammar, code, reasoning steps) depends on this signal.

Example: sinusoidal encodings add a unique wave-pattern vector per position; learned encodings learn one vector per position up to the max length.

Common mistake: assuming absolute positions generalize past the training length — they don't, which is why RoPE + interpolation exist.
sections.intermediate:
How: absolute (sinusoidal/learned, added to embeddings), relative (bias by distance, T5-style), RoPE (rotate Q/K by position — relative information through absolute rotations), ALiBi (linear penalty by distance, extrapolates well).

Rule: RoPE is the default for new models (LLaMA/Mistral/Qwen). ALiBi if you care about zero-shot length extrapolation without retuning.

Trade-off: learned absolute = simplest, hard-capped length; RoPE = best quality-per-effort, needs interpolation tricks past training length.
sections.advanced:
Implementation: extending context: NTK-aware scaling (redistribute rotary frequencies instead of naive interpolation), YaRN (ramped mix + temperature fix), continued training on long docs after scaling (a few B tokens teaches the new range).

Failure modes: naive position interpolation collapses long-context quality (perplexity explodes past ~2× trained length); forgetting to scale RoPE theta when fine-tuning long-context.
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: RoPE rotates each 2D slice of q/k by angle m·θᵢ where m is position and θᵢ = base^(−2i/d). Attention then depends on (m−n) — relative distance falls out of the rotation difference. Extrapolation fails because unseen large m hit untrained angular velocities at high frequencies; NTK-aware scaling lowers the base so frequencies redistribute into the trained regime.

title: Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE)
summary: The position encoding used by LLaMA, Mistral, and most modern models.

sections.beginner:
What: RoPE (Rotary Positional Embeddings) rotates query and key vectors by position-dependent angles before attention, so the score between two tokens depends on their relative distance.

Why: it replaced absolute encodings in LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen, and nearly every modern open model — better quality and no learned position table to cap length.

Example: token at position 5 gets its Q rotated by 5·θ; token at 2 by 2·θ; their dot product sees the difference (3·θ) — relative position, computed from absolute rotations.
sections.intermediate:
How: split q/k into pairs, rotate each pair by (position × frequency); frequencies decay geometrically across dims (θᵢ = base^(−2i/d), base usually 10k–500k). Apply before the QK dot product, never to values.

Rule: larger theta (e.g., 500k) supports longer contexts out of the box — check the model's rope_theta in config before extending context yourself.
sections.advanced:
Implementation: long-context extension = scale frequencies (linear interpolation, NTK-aware, or YaRN) + short continued training on long documents. YaRN adds a temperature correction on the attention logits that plain interpolation lacks.

Failure modes: scaling without continued training (works to ~2–4×, degrades after); mismatched theta between base model and fine-tune (silently wrong positions).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: full derivation: with rotation matrices R(m), q′=R(m)q, k′=R(n)k, and q′·k′ = qᵀR(n−m)k — relative shift appears exactly. High-frequency dims (large θᵢ) encode fine position but alias beyond trained m; low-frequency dims carry coarse position. NTK theory says interpolate by changing the base so the spectral coverage matches training — which is why theta-scaling beats position-scaling at large factors.

title: Feed-Forward Networks (FFN)

sections.beginner:
What: after attention mixes information across tokens, the FFN transforms each token independently: hidden → wide (×3–4) → nonlinearity → back to hidden. Two-thirds of a typical LLM's params live here.

Why: attention routes; the FFN computes. Most factual recall ('Paris is the capital of…') is attributed to FFN layers acting as key-value memories.

Example: LLaMA-3-8B: 32 layers × ~135M FFN params ≈ 4.3B — over half the model.

Common mistake: shrinking the FFN to save memory while keeping attention wide — quality per param favors balanced scaling.
sections.intermediate:
How: expansion ratio (wide ÷ hidden): GPT-style 4×, LLaMA/SwiGLU ~3.5× (gated FFNs use smaller ratios since they have 3 matrices). Param share ≈ FFN ÷ total ≈ 60–70%.

Rule: when sizing a custom model in the Model Calculator, set the FFN first from your param budget — it dominates the count.
sections.advanced: Implementation: SwiGLU/GEGLU gating (gate ⊙ up, then down) beats plain ReLU-FFN at scale; fused gate+up matmuls save a pass; MoE replaces the dense FFN with routed experts for sparse scaling.
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: per-token FFN FLOPs = 2 × FFN params (multiply-add) — the FFN dominates both params and compute. Expansion-ratio ablations show quality saturates past ~4× (dense) / ~3.5× (gated); further capacity is better spent on depth. Memory note: FFN activations are the largest single activation tensor — the first target of checkpointing.

summary: The per-token dense layers holding most of the model's params.

title: SwiGLU FFN

sections.beginner:
What: SwiGLU replaces the plain FFN with a gated version: two parallel projections, one passed through SiLU (smooth S-curve), multiplied together, then projected back. Three matrices instead of two.

Why: the gate lets the network dynamically suppress or amplify features per token — consistently better quality at 7B+ than plain FFNs, now standard in LLaMA/Mistral/Qwen.

Example: out = down(silu(gate(x)) * up(x)) — one extra matmul, measurable eval gains.
sections.intermediate:
How: sizes: gate and up are hidden → ffn_hidden; down is ffn_hidden → hidden; ffn_hidden ≈ 8/3 × hidden adjusted to a multiple (LLaMA) or ~3.5×. Params = 3 × hidden × ffn_hidden.

Rule: if your Model Calculator FFN estimate looks 1.5× too big vs a LLaMA-style config, you forgot SwiGLU has 3 matrices, not 2.
sections.advanced: Implementation: GEGLU (GELU gate) and ReGLU (ReLU gate) variants trade smoothness for sparsity/recompute cost; fused silu-mul kernels matter for inference latency; some quantized kernels only support specific gated shapes — verify before committing.
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: gating produces input-dependent effective weights (multiplicative interaction = second-order-ish expressiveness per layer), which explains the sample-efficiency win. Sparsity view: ReGLU zeroes negatives outright (activation sparsity exploitable by sparse kernels); SiLU keeps smooth gradients (better optimization). FP16 note: the gate×up product can spike magnitudes — another quiet argument for BF16 training with gated FFNs.

summary: Gated FFN variant standard in LLaMA, Mistral, and Qwen.

title: Residual Connections

sections.beginner:
What: each sub-layer adds its output to its input: x = x + Sublayer(Norm(x)). Information (and gradients) can skip past any layer untouched.

Why: without skips, gradients shrink through dozens of layers and deep nets stop learning. Residuals are why 100-layer models train at all.

Example: remove all residuals from a 24-layer transformer and it degrades to ~shallow-net quality even with perfect tuning.

Common mistake: post-norm placement in a deep self-trained model (unstable without careful init) — use pre-norm.
sections.intermediate:
How: pre-norm (norm inside the branch — stable, standard) vs post-norm (norm after the add — stronger peak in shallow nets, fragile deep). The residual stream accumulates layer outputs additively.

Rule: pre-norm for anything you train beyond ~12 layers; scale the residual (DeepNorm) past ~100 layers.
sections.advanced: Implementation: stochastic depth drops whole residual branches during training (depth-wise dropout); LayerScale/ReZero learn per-branch gates; norm-free designs (NFNets-style) exist but never caught on for LLMs.
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: interpret the residual stream as shared working memory: each head/FFN reads from it and writes additive updates. Unembedding analyses (logit lens) show predictions sharpening progressively along the stream. Gradient view: the identity path gives every layer a direct, unattenuated gradient signal — depth without decay.

summary: Skip connections that make deep networks trainable.

title: The Transformer Block

sections.beginner:
What: one block = masked attention sub-layer + FFN sub-layer, each wrapped as add-and-norm. Stack 12–100 of them, add embeddings at the bottom and an output head on top: that is an LLM.

Why: the block cleanly separates the two jobs — attention moves info between positions, FFN processes within positions — repeated until representations are rich enough to predict the next token.

Example: GPT-2-small: 12 blocks × 768 hidden ≈ 124M params. LLaMA-3-8B: 32 blocks × 4096 hidden ≈ 8B.
sections.intermediate:
How: variants: decoder-only (causal mask, generation — GPT/LLaMA), encoder-only (bidirectional, classification/embeddings — BERT), encoder-decoder (translation-style, T5). Pre-norm decoder-only is the modern default.

Rule: new project? Decoder-only + pre-norm + RoPE + RMSNorm + SwiGLU — the converged recipe; deviate only for a measured reason.
sections.advanced: Implementation: parallel block (attention and FFN computed concurrently from the same normed input — PaLM/Falcon, saves a sync point), interleaved/sliding attention layers for long context, layer dropping for inference speed.
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: capacity analysis: per-block params ≈ 4h² (attn, MHA) + 3·e·h² (SwiGLU FFN) where e = expansion. Depth-vs-width: depth composes (reasoning steps), width memorizes (facts) — reasoning benchmarks favor deeper thinner models at fixed params, within stability limits. Representation bounds are dominated by residual-stream width × depth.

summary: Attention plus FFN, stacked: the anatomy of an LLM layer.

title: Decoder-Only Architecture

sections.beginner:
What: decoder-only models read left-to-right with a causal mask and predict the next token. GPT, LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen — every model you will fine-tune — are decoder-only.

Why: next-token prediction on raw text needs no labels, so it scales to trillions of tokens. That scalability beat fancier architectures.

Example: training sample 'The cat sat' → predict 'cat' from 'The', 'sat' from 'The cat', all positions in one forward pass (parallel teacher forcing).

Common mistake: fine-tuning a base decoder without a chat template and expecting instruction behavior — the capability is latent until SFT formats it.
sections.intermediate:
How: vs encoder-decoder: decoder-only is simpler (one stack), better-studied at scale, and unifies pretraining + SFT + DPO in one objective. Encoder-decoder retains niches (some retrieval/translation setups) but has lost the ecosystem.

Rule: default to decoder-only unless you inherit an encoder-decoder pipeline with measured wins.
sections.advanced: Implementation: efficient variants keep the interface (causal LM loss) while changing internals: sliding-window attention (Mistral), linear/recurrent alternatives (Mamba/RWKV) for cheap long context, hybrid attention-SSM stacks.
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: decoder-only training is maximum likelihood over factorizations p(x)=∏p(xᵢ|x<ᵢ) — every position is a training signal (dense supervision), unlike masked LM's 15%. Scaling analyses attribute decoder-only's dominance to this density plus inference simplicity (one KV cache, one code path). Expressiveness is Turing-complete given chain-of-thought scratchpad — depth + generation steps substitute for architectural complexity.

summary: Causal next-token architecture behind GPT, LLaMA, and friends.

title: Causal (Masked) Attention

sections.beginner:
What: the triangular mask that hides future tokens: position i may use tokens 0…i only. The −∞ entries become zero after softmax.

Why: without it the model cheats — peeking at the answer it must predict. Train unmasked and eval looks miraculous while real generation is gibberish (train/inference mismatch).

Example: 4-token mask rows: [1,0,0,0], [1,1,0,0], [1,1,1,0], [1,1,1,1] — each row is 'what this position may see'.

Common mistake: custom mask with wrong dtype in FP16 (use additive −inf bias, not large negatives that overflow).
sections.intermediate:
How: boolean vs additive-bias implementations (bias is safer across backends); FlashAttention fuses the causal pattern (no N² mask materialized); sliding-window = banded causal (each token sees the last W).

Rule: verify causality with a chew test: shift inputs by one and confirm outputs shift identically (or check a diagonal-leak probe) before long runs.
sections.advanced: Implementation: document masks for packed sequences (block-diagonal: sequences in a packed batch must not see each other — without it, packing leaks across documents); prefix-LM masks (bidirectional prefix + causal suffix) for infilling models.
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: the causal operator is lower-triangular; its interaction with KV cache is exact (append-only state). Packed-sequence masks are block-diagonal triangular — implementation via segment IDs + fused kernels (flash_attn_varlen). Leak bugs here are catastrophic and silent: loss drops (the model 'predicts' using leaked futures) while generation quality is poor — always compare packed vs unpacked loss on a probe batch.

summary: The triangular mask that prevents peeking at the future.

title: Dataset Engineering

sections.beginner:
What: dataset engineering turns raw text into training-ready tokens: ingest → clean → filter → dedup → mix → tokenize → split → validate. Data quality beats data quantity — a filtered 100B tokens routinely beats raw 1T.

Why: models memorize garbage as faithfully as gold. Duplicates, boilerplate, and leaked test data silently inflate scores while hurting real ability.

Example: 100 GB raw Common-Crawl-style text → ~40 GB after exact+near dedup → ~25 GB after quality filtering → tokenize (~0.25 tokens/byte English) ≈ 6B tokens.

Common mistake: counting raw file size as 'training data' — report post-filter tokens; bytes lie (markup, duplicates, wrong languages).
sections.intermediate:
How: JSONL/Parquet pipelines; language ID; perplexity/quality classifiers for filtering; MinHash+LSH near-dedup; PII/toxicity screens; domain mixing ratios; held-out splits cut before any filtering tuned on them.

Rule: dedup exact first (cheap, big win), then near-dedup (expensive, quality win), then model-based filtering (most expensive, tune the threshold on a small train probe).

Trade-off: aggressive filtering raises quality-per-token but can erase dialects, code, or rare domains — track domain shares before/after each stage.
sections.advanced:
Implementation: web-scale pipelines (streaming, sharded, resumable); synthetic data generation with diversity controls + decontamination against evals; mixture search (DoReMi-style learned weights); dataset versioning (hash + manifest + code that built it).

Failure modes: near-dup threshold too tight (memorized benchmarks leak through paraphrases); filter classifier trained on its own outputs (collapse loop); undocumented regeneration (unreproducible runs).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: MinHash approximates Jaccard similarity with k smallest hashes; LSH bands find candidate pairs in sub-quadratic time — the only feasible route at trillion-token scale. Economics: data work has the highest ROI per engineer-hour in most LLM projects because every downstream step (compute, eval, serving) amortizes over the same tokens.

summary: Turning raw text into training-ready tokens.

title: Data Cleaning & Filtering

sections.beginner:
What: removing what hurts: repeated lines, boilerplate menus, wrong-language pages, HTML/JS residue, extreme-length outliers, empty docs.

Why: a model trained on navigation bars learns to emit navigation bars. Cleaning is teaching by example selection.

Example: heuristics that work: drop docs with >30% duplicate lines, <50 words, symbol-to-word ratio >0.3, or failed language-ID confidence.

Common mistake: regex-only cleaning of HTML — use a parser; regexes leave script fragments that become 'knowledge'.
sections.intermediate:
How: staged filters (cheap heuristics → language ID → perplexity/quality scorers → LLM judges on samples); length windows per domain (code tolerates long, chat doesn't); code filtering (compile/parse check, license allow-list).

Rule: calibrate each filter on 500 hand-labeled docs before running at scale — measure precision/recall of the filter itself.
sections.advanced:
Implementation: perplexity filtering with a small reference model (keep the middle band — too predictable = boilerplate, too surprising = noise); LLM-judge pipelines with rubrics + adjudication; human-in-the-loop audits per data release.

Failure modes: perplexity filters biased against dialects/minority language (high-PPL ≠ low-quality); over-cleaning code (removing the 'messy' real-world patterns the model must handle).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: the cleaning trade-off is a bias-variance choice on the data distribution: aggressive cleaning shrinks support (safer, narrower model), conservative cleaning keeps tails (capable, riskier). Track the filtering funnel as a distribution shift report — share histograms of kept vs dropped by domain, length, and language — so capability gaps stay explainable.

summary: Removing what hurts: boilerplate, noise, and wrong-language text.

title: Data Contamination

sections.beginner:
What: contamination = test/benchmark text inside training data. The model 'scores well' by recall, not reasoning — the score is a lie.

Why: web-scale corpora swallow benchmarks whole (MMLU/GSM8K text is all over the web). A contaminated +5% means nothing and misleads every downstream decision.

Example: GSM8K-style problems quoted in blogs, then crawled into pretraining → the model memorized solutions; held-out paraphrases reveal the gap.

Common mistake: 'we filtered exact matches, so we're clean' — paraphrases and templated variants sail through exact filters.
sections.intermediate:
How: exact-match (hash/n-gram overlap vs eval sets), fuzzy match (high n-gram overlap, embedding similarity), canary strings (benchmark authors plant GUIDs — grep your corpus for them), paraphrase probes (score drops on reworded items ⇒ memorization).

Rule: decontaminate against every benchmark you report, with both exact and ≥13-gram overlap removal, and disclose the method.
sections.advanced: Implementation: perfect detection at web scale is impossible (paraphrase space is unbounded) — defense in depth: crawl exclusion + aggressive dedup vs eval corpora + private held-out sets + dynamic evals (fresh items per run, e.g., live-code or dated questions).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: systematic studies find contamination inflates scores roughly with match density and model size (bigger models memorize more). Open question: where memorization ends and 'training on the task distribution' begins — the community answer is procedural: held-out, dated, and private evals are the only scores you can trust for decisions.

summary: Test data leaking into training, and how to fight it.

title: Licensing for Models & Datasets
summary: What you may train on, ship, and sell — the basics.

sections.beginner:
What: three license layers: data licenses (web text ≠ free-to-train everywhere; code licenses vary — MIT/Apache vs GPL), model licenses (Apache/MIT = permissive; LLaMA/Gemma community = use-restricted; check redistribution + commercial clauses), and your obligations (attribution, share-alike, acceptable-use).

Why: license violations surface at the worst moment (funding, launch, enterprise deal). 'Open weights' ≠ 'open for my use case' — read the actual license.

Example: Mistral-7B Apache 2.0 (commercial OK, permissive) vs LLaMA-3 Community (commercial allowed with conditions + monthly-user threshold) vs GPL code in training data (copyleft risk for code models).

Common mistake: assuming 'publicly downloadable' means 'licensed for commercial training' — it does not.
sections.intermediate:
