How: per-document license classes tracked through the pipeline (allow/deny/review lists); code-data license filters (exclude strong-copyleft for commercial code models); model-card obligations honored (attribution files, use-policy enforcement points); synthetic-data provenance (generated from X under Y terms).

Rule: gate releases mechanically on license metadata — human memory doesn't scale to billion-document corpora.
sections.advanced: Implementation: dataset manifests with license histograms; PII + license joint review for releases; enterprise artifact (SBOM-for-data: sources, licenses, transforms); policy for takedown requests and retroactive exclusions (rebuildable pipeline required).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: the legal landscape (training-data fair-use/text-and-data-mining exemptions) varies by jurisdiction and is actively litigated — this topic states practice, not legal advice. Engineering stance: minimize exposure (respect robots/opt-outs, filter copyleft where it matters, document everything) so legal questions have factual answers. Consult counsel for product decisions; treat VERIFY labels here as load-bearing.

title: Deduplication

sections.beginner:
What: duplicates teach the model to repeat: memorized passages, inflated eval scores, wasted compute (paying to train on the same text twice).

Why: web text is ~30–60% near-duplicate (quotes, syndication, templates). Removing it is the cheapest quality-per-FLOP win in the pipeline.

Example: exact dedup by document hash first (kills copies), then near-dedup (kills reposts with edits) — expect 20–50% token reduction on crawled data.

Common mistake: deduping after tokenization/shuffling — dedup raw text first, or identical docs with different token boundaries survive.
sections.intermediate:
How: exact (SHA/hash of normalized text), near (MinHash signatures + LSH banding, Jaccard threshold ~0.8), document-level (drop whole dup docs) vs shard-level; cross-split dedup (train vs val/test overlap removal is mandatory).

Rule: always dedup train against eval sets, not just train against itself — self-dedup doesn't fix contamination.

Trade-off: threshold too loose keeps spam; too tight deletes legitimately similar docs (legal boilerplate, code patterns). Tune on samples.
sections.advanced:
Implementation: web-scale via distributed MinHash (signature sharding), Bloom filters for streaming exact-dedup at TB scale, URL+content composite keys (same content, new URL still counts).

Failure modes: LSH parameter misconfiguration (recall collapse — most near-dups missed silently); normalizing away meaningful differences (code with different constants hashes equal under aggressive normalization).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: MinHash: P(same min-hash) = Jaccard similarity — k hashes give a similarity estimate with error O(1/√k). LSH banding (b bands × r rows) creates an S-curve threshold ≈ (1/b)^(1/r): pairs above it are near-certain candidates. Complexity drops from O(N²) comparisons to ~O(N) — the enabling trick for trillion-token corpora.

summary: Exact and near-duplicate removal at scale.

title: Data Mixing, Splits & Versioning
summary: Ratios, leakage-free splits, and releases you can reproduce.

sections.beginner:
What: mixing = what share of each domain (web/code/books/chat); splits = train/val/test carved before tuning anything; versioning = every release hashed, manifested, and rebuildable.

Why: mix sets the model's personality (code-heavy → better code, worse prose); leaky splits (near-dups across train/test) fake quality; unversioned data makes runs irreproducible.

Example: 50% web / 20% code / 15% books / 10% academic / 5% chat is a sane general starting mix — then adjust by eval gaps.
sections.intermediate:
How: split by document clusters + time (not random lines — random splits leak near-dups); dedup across splits; mixture search (train small probes per mix candidate, pick by target evals); lock test before training, disclose it.

Rule: no filter threshold, mix ratio, or template is tuned on test. Ever. Val decides, test reports.

Trade-off: domain upsampling fixes weaknesses fast but over-concentrates style (code models that answer prose in code blocks) — cap any domain ≤ ~40% without a measured reason.
sections.advanced: Implementation: learned mixtures (DoReMi/group-DRO on proxy models); synthetic-data ratios (cap ~10–30%, decontaminate, label provenance); manifests (per-file hashes, pipeline code hash, filter params) + dataset cards (license, PII stance, known gaps).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: mixture effects are approximately log-linear in domain tokens (more of domain X → predictable gains on X-evals, predictable decay elsewhere) — measurable with small-scale mix sweeps that transfer surprisingly well. Provenance/licensing is a first-class field: track per-document license class through every stage so releases can exclude copyleft/PII segments mechanically, not by memory.

title: Pretraining Fundamentals

sections.beginner:
What: pretraining teaches a randomly-initialized model next-token prediction on trillions of tokens. Output: a base model with broad knowledge but no instruction manners.

Why: this is where capabilities come from — reasoning patterns, facts, languages, code. Everything after (SFT/LoRA/DPO) only steers what pretraining built.

Example: LLaMA-3-8B: ~15T tokens, months on thousands of H100s. Your 100M practice model: ~1B tokens, hours on one 24 GB GPU — same loop, different scale.

Common mistake: starting a 'pretrain from scratch' project to fix what SFT on a good open base would solve in an afternoon.
sections.intermediate:
How: token budget first (Chinchilla: ~20 tokens/param, modern practice often 100+ for smaller models), batch in tokens/step (0.5–4M for 1–8B), LR peak ~3e-4 (7B) with 1–3% warmup + cosine decay, BF16 + AdamW, checkpoint every ~1B tokens.

Rule: steps = total_tokens ÷ tokens_per_step. A 1B-token run at 0.5M tokens/step = 2,000 steps — plan LR horizon and checkpoint cadence from that number.

Trade-off: more tokens/param beats more params/token under a fixed FLOP budget (Chinchilla) — but inference cost favors smaller models trained longer.
sections.advanced:
Implementation: stability kit: warmup, grad clip 1.0, BF16 (not FP16), attention backend checks, loss-spike protocol (skip step, rollback to last good checkpoint if persistent, lower LR 2× on repeat); data-mix scheduling (curriculum/heavy-code phases); MFU target 40–60%.

Failure modes: loss spike → NaN cascade (usually LR/batch too aggressive for the width); silent divergence (loss falls, downstream flat — data mix or tokenizer bug); mid-run data exhaustion (repeating <1 epoch of unique data on large models).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: scaling laws L(N,D) = E + A/N^α + B/D^β fit loss vs params (N) and tokens (D) — compute-optimal frontier where marginal loss-per-FLOP equalizes. Emergence debate: some 'jumps' are metric artifacts (nonlinear/discontinuous metrics on smooth loss curves). Economics: pretraining cost ≈ 6·N·D FLOPs ÷ (achieved FLOP/s) — estimate feasibility with the planners before anything else.

summary: Next-token training that builds base-model capability.

title: Fine-Tuning

sections.beginner:
What: fine-tuning continues training a pretrained model on your data to change behavior (follow instructions) or add domain skill. Full fine-tuning updates all weights; LoRA/QLoRA update small adapters.

Why: base models complete text; fine-tuning makes them answer, refuse, format JSON, write in your house style. Almost every shipped LLM behavior comes from this stage.

Example: 10k instruction pairs × 3 epochs on LLaMA-3-8B with LoRA r=16 — an evening on one RTX 4090.

Common mistake: full-FT learning rates on an instruct model (destroys prior alignment fast) — fine-tune LR ≈ 1/10th–1/3rd of pretraining peak, with warmup.
sections.intermediate:
How: SFT format (prompt + response, loss on response tokens only — mask the prompt), 1–3 epochs, batch 32–128 sequences, LR 1e-5–2e-4, eval on held-out instructions + general benchmarks (watch forgetting).

Rule: if general-benchmark scores fall while task scores rise, you are trading, not improving — cut LR/epochs or mix in general data (5–20%).

Trade-off: full FT = max adaptation, max memory/forgetting risk; LoRA = ~1% trainable, mergeable, forgets less; QLoRA = LoRA on a 4-bit base, cheapest.
sections.advanced:
Implementation: continued pretraining (raw domain text, LR ~10% of pretrain) BEFORE SFT when the domain is knowledge-heavy (medicine, law, code) — SFT teaches format, CPT teaches facts; multi-task mixing to preserve breadth; replay buffers against catastrophic forgetting.

Failure modes: format leakage (model answers everything in the SFT template); length exploitation (long responses rewarded by lazy evals); tokenizer/template mismatch between train and serve.
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: fine-tuning moves weights a small distance in a flat basin — linear mode connectivity explains why merging (adapters, model soups) works. Forgetting is gradient interference: new-task gradients have negative dot product with old-task directions; replay and low LRs keep the walk inside the intersection of good regions. Empirical guideline: adaptation rank needed grows with distribution shift — near-domain shifts are low-rank (LoRA territory), new languages/modalities often aren't.

summary: Adapting pretrained models to tasks and domains.

title: SFT Data Formatting
summary: Chat templates, masking, and packing — the details SFT quality lives in.

sections.beginner:
What: SFT examples must look exactly like serving: the model's chat template (system/user/assistant markers), with loss computed on assistant tokens only (prompt masked out).

Why: unmasked SFT teaches the model to predict prompts (weird, servile completions); wrong template at train vs serve silently costs 10–30% instruction-following.

Example: apply tokenizer.apply_chat_template(messages) for both training and inference — never hand-roll the markers.
sections.intermediate:
How: response-only masking (labels = −100 on prompt/system/control tokens); packing short conversations to seq length with document masks (or pad — packing without masks leaks across examples); multi-turn: mask user turns, train on all assistant turns (weight final turns if they matter most).

Rule: decode a few training samples and eyeball them — template bugs are visible in seconds to eyes and invisible to loss.
sections.advanced: Implementation: tool-call/response formatting (strict schemas, thought/action separation); refusal + safety exemplars in-template; length balancing (avoid teaching verbosity via long-chosen bias); packing + FlashAttention varlen for efficiency without leakage.
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: masking changes the gradient support (only response positions pull weights) — unmasked SFT wastes ~50%+ of gradient signal on prompt tokens and shifts the learned distribution toward prompt style. Template tokens are high-frequency anchors: the model binds behavior to their exact IDs, which is why a single changed marker at serve time can collapse compliance.

title: Continued Pretraining (CPT)
summary: When to keep pretraining vs when to SFT — and how to not destroy the model.

sections.beginner:
What: CPT = more next-token training on domain raw text (papers, code, another language) before any instruction tuning. SFT teaches format; CPT teaches facts.

When CPT over SFT: the model lacks domain knowledge (new language, medicine, proprietary codebase) or domain perplexity is far above general — SFT cannot install missing knowledge, only style.

Example: 5–50B domain tokens at ~10% of pretrain LR, mixed with 5–20% general data (replay), then SFT as usual.

Common mistake: CPT on a tiny corpus at full LR (catastrophic forgetting in an afternoon) — small data + small LR + replay, or skip CPT.
sections.intermediate:
How: LR ≈ 0.1× pretrain peak with short warmup + decay; replay general data (5–20%) to anchor capabilities; monitor general benchmarks alongside domain PPL (trade, don't just gain); quality-filter the domain corpus first (CPT amplifies garbage into 'knowledge').

Rule: decide by measurement: if domain val-PPL of the base is terrible AND SFT alone doesn't fix task scores, CPT earns its cost. Otherwise SFT/LoRA.
sections.advanced: Implementation: vocabulary extension for new languages/scripts (add tokens, init from similar, brief embedding-focused tuning); staged CPT (broad domain → narrow specialty); CPT + LoRA hybrids (frozen-base CPT via adapters exists but lags full CPT for heavy shifts).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: forgetting is gradient interference on shared directions; replay works by keeping old-task gradients in the batch (positive dot products preserved). LR scaling follows from basin geometry: pretrained basins are flat and wide — small steps stay inside (retain + adapt), large steps exit (forget). Rank analysis: domain shifts needing high-rank updates (new languages) resist LoRA-scale adaptation — the mechanistic reason CPT-vs-LoRA decisions hinge on shift size.

title: LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation)

sections.beginner:
What: LoRA freezes the 7B base model and trains tiny add-on matrices per layer: instead of updating W (4096×4096), train A (4096×16) × B (16×4096) and add W + (α/r)·BA. Trainable params drop ~100×.

Why it uses less memory: gradients + Adam states exist only for the adapters (~10–50M params), not the 7B base. Base weights need no gradients, no optimizer state — just storage (quantizable, see QLoRA).

Example: 7B + r=16 on attention+MLP ≈ 20–40M trainable (~0.5%). Fits fine-tuning on a 24 GB GPU that could never full-FT 7B.

Common mistake: r=1–4 on hard tasks then concluding 'LoRA doesn't work' — rank is capacity; start r=16–32, α=2r.
sections.intermediate:
How: rank r (capacity: 8/16/32/64), alpha α (the update is scaled by α/r — so α=2r means 2x scaling, α=r means 1x; rsLoRA uses α/√r for high ranks), dropout (0–0.1), target modules (start: q,k,v,o + gate,up,down — all-linear beats attention-only on most tasks), LR ~1e-4–2e-4, merge (BA into W) for zero-latency inference or keep unmerged for multi-adapter serving.

Rule: hard task or big shift → raise r (32–64) and target all linear layers before touching LR. More data beats more rank past r=64.

Trade-off: LoRA ≈ full-FT quality on near-domain tasks; gap widens for new languages, long-form reasoning shifts, and heavy memorization (new facts prefer CPT or higher rank).
sections.advanced:
Implementation: DoRA (magnitude+direction decomposition, small gains), rsLoRA (stabilized scaling α/√r for high ranks), PiSSA/MoRA (better init/subspaces), multi-adapter routing (one base, many LoRAs switched per request).

Failure modes: underfitting at low rank on knowledge-heavy tasks (fix: CPT first or full FT); merged-adapter dtype mismatch (merge in FP32/BF16, not INT); eval with the adapter detached (scores the base model — verify active adapters).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: the low-rank assumption: fine-tuning updates ΔW have rapidly decaying singular spectra on near-domain tasks (intrinsic dimension ≪ full rank) — LoRA parameterizes exactly that subspace. Memory math: full-FT BF16 Adam ≈ 16 B/param (2 weight + 4 master + 2 grad + 8 states); LoRA pays that only on adapters while the base costs just storage (2 B/param BF16, ~0.5–0.6 B/param NF4 with scales). When the shift is high-rank (new language), the assumption breaks — hence full-FT/CPT wins there.

summary: Low-rank adapters: fine-tune 7B models on one GPU.

title: QLoRA

sections.beginner:
What: QLoRA = LoRA on a 4-bit-quantized base model. The 7B base shrinks from ~14 GB (BF16) to ~4–5 GB (NF4 with scales/metadata), so adapters + optimizer fit on a single 8–12 GB GPU.

Why it fits what FP16 cannot: FP16 7B needs ~112 GB to full-FT (weights+master+grads+states); QLoRA pays 4-bit storage for the frozen base and full-precision training only on ~0.5% adapter params — total often <10 GB.

Example: LLaMA-3-8B NF4 + r=32 adapters + BF16 compute: trains on an RTX 3060-12GB with batch 1–2 + grad accumulation.

Common mistake: quantizing the adapters too (keep adapters + compute in BF16 — only the frozen base is 4-bit).
sections.intermediate:
How: NF4 (quantile-normalized 4-bit — matches normal-distributed weights better than INT4), double quantization (quantize the quantization constants, saves ~0.4 bits/param), paged optimizers (spill spikes to CPU instead of OOM), BF16 compute dtype, LR ~2e-4.

Rule: recipe — load_in_4bit + NF4 + bfloat16 compute + r=32/α=64 + grad accumulation to ≥32 seq effective batch — then tune data first, rank second.

Trade-off: small quality gap vs full LoRA (quantization noise in the frozen base); gap grows for math/code precision tasks — verify on your eval, not vibes.
sections.advanced: Implementation: NF4 vs INT4/FP4 (NF4 usually wins for normal weights); which modules to keep unquantized (embeddings/norms stay high precision); QLoRA + FSDP/CPU-offload for 33–70B on workstations; merging 4-bit base + adapters needs dequantize-merge-requantize (or serve unmerged).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: the QLoRA paper's accounting: 7B full-FT ≈ 112+ GB vs QLoRA ≈ 6–10 GB with ≈99% of quality retained on instruction tasks. Why it works: frozen-base quantization noise is static (no error accumulation through optimizer steps) while adapters train in full precision and absorb residual error. Limits: tasks needing precise base-weight memorization (rare facts, exact arithmetic circuits) suffer most — noise floor ≈ half an NF4 bin per weight.

summary: LoRA on a 4-bit base: big-model tuning on small GPUs.

title: RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback)

sections.beginner:
What: RLHF = train a reward model on human preferences, then optimize the LLM against it with RL (PPO), anchored by a KL penalty to stay near the original model. The InstructGPT/ChatGPT recipe.

Why: it aligns behavior (helpful, harmless, honest) beyond what imitation (SFT) can express — preferences over outputs are richer supervision than single demonstrations.

Example: rank 4 sampled answers per prompt → reward model learns the ranking → PPO nudges the policy toward high-reward regions.

Common mistake: attempting PPO before exhausting SFT + DPO — 90% of alignment gains come cheaper.
sections.intermediate:
How: pipeline: SFT → preference collection → reward model (pairwise accuracy ≥65–70% or fix data) → PPO (clip range, KL coefficient ~0.01–0.1, value-loss coeffs) → eval on alignment + capability suites (KL drift destroys the latter first).

Rule: the reward model is the ceiling — a 60%-accurate RM trains a worse policy no matter how good the PPO. Validate the RM independently.
sections.advanced:
Implementation: reward hacking defenses (KL anchor, RM ensembles, held-out RM for eval), RLAIF (AI-labeled preferences at scale, then spot-check with humans), online variants (GRPO/RLOO drop the value network); when DPO suffices (static pairs, no exploration need) vs when RLHF wins (open-ended tasks needing exploration).

Failure modes: PPO instability (clip/KL mis-tuning → collapse); RM over-optimization (proxy score up, human judgment down — Goodhart in action); forgetting (KL too loose erases pretraining).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: PPO's clipped surrogate bounds policy movement per step while the KL term bounds total drift from the SFT anchor — the tension between them is the whole game. Reproducibility is poor because outcomes depend on rollout sampling, RM seed, and KL schedule jointly. Current direction: simpler online methods (GRPO) and process supervision (rewarding reasoning steps, not just outcomes).

summary: Reward-model plus PPO alignment pipeline.

title: DPO (Direct Preference Optimization)

sections.beginner:
What: DPO aligns models from preference pairs (prompt + chosen + rejected response) with a plain classification-style loss — no reward model, no RL, no PPO rollout loop.

Why: RLHF needs three models and fragile RL tuning; DPO needs two (policy + frozen reference) and standard supervised tooling. Most teams should try DPO first.

Example: 10k human-ranked pairs → DPO on your SFT model, β=0.1, 1 epoch — helpfulness/harmlessness lift without an RL stack.

Common mistake: DPO on noisy/auto-labeled pairs — preference noise teaches the margin directly; curate pairs before scaling them.
sections.intermediate:
How: loss pushes log-prob(chosen) above log-prob(rejected) relative to the reference model, with β controlling sharpness (0.05–0.5; lower = stronger). Data: chosen/rejected must differ in the behavior you want (style-only pairs teach verbosity).

Rule: watch the margin (chosen−rejected logprob), not just loss — healthy DPO raises the margin; collapsing likelihoods on both sides signal trouble.

Trade-off: DPO is offline/simple but bounded by pair coverage; online RL (PPO/GRPO) explores beyond the dataset at much higher complexity.
sections.advanced:
Implementation: IPO/KTO/ORPO variants (IPO resists overfitting to deterministic pairs; KTO works without paired rejects; ORPO skips the reference model); length-normalization to fight verbosity bias; mixing SFT data during DPO to anchor capabilities.

Failure modes: likelihood collapse (both responses fall — raise β or shorten training); length hacking (chosen longer on average → model bloats outputs — normalize or balance lengths); reference-model mismatch (DPO against the wrong base distorts the KL anchor).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: DPO reparameterizes the Bradley-Terry + KL-constrained RL optimum into a direct loss: the optimal policy has closed form in terms of reward, so fitting rewards ≡ fitting the policy margin. Equivalence with RLHF holds under the same preference model and coverage — in practice they differ because online RL samples off-policy responses while DPO never leaves the dataset support. Choose by data regime: fixed pairs → DPO; reward model + exploration budget → RL.

summary: Preference alignment without reinforcement learning.

title: Evaluation Methods

sections.beginner:
What: evaluation answers 'did the model get better?' — loss curves cannot. Use task benchmarks (MMLU knowledge, GSM8K math, HumanEval code, IFEval instruction-following) plus your own held-out task set.

Why: training loss can fall while real ability stalls or regresses (memorization, format overfitting, forgetting). Loss measures fit; evals measure capability.

Example: after SFT: task win-rate up +12%, MMLU −1% (acceptable trade), GSM8K flat — ship. MMLU −6%? You traded brains for manners — fix the mix.

Common mistake: reporting only the benchmark that went up (cherry-picking) or evaluating on training-adjacent data.
sections.intermediate:
How: pick suites covering your claim (knowledge/reasoning/code/instruction-following), few-shot protocol fixed across runs, greedy decoding for comparability, baselines (base model + prior checkpoint), contamination screening vs your train data.

Rule: every reported number needs: exact harness version, shots, decoding, and whether train data was screened against the eval. Otherwise it is not a number, it is a rumor.

Trade-off: public benchmarks (comparable, possibly contaminated) vs private held-outs (trustworthy, incomparable externally) — run both.
sections.advanced:
Implementation: regression gates in CI (fine-tune PRs must not drop core suites), dynamic evals (fresh items — dated questions, live code tasks), LLM-judge evals with rubrics + human calibration (report judge agreement), custom task sets mirroring production traffic.

Failure modes: harness drift (version bumps change scores silently — pin everything); prompt-sensitivity (rankings flip with formatting — average over templates); saturated benchmarks (all models >90% — the test stopped measuring).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: benchmark scores are noisy estimators: binomial error ≈ √(p(1−p)/n) — a 1% MMLU delta on 14k items is ~±0.5%, often indistinguishable from seed noise. The 'evaluation crisis': static public tests get trained into models (directly or via distillation), so scores inflate while true capability lags. Response: private held-outs, prospective (future-dated) evals, and capability-probing (counterfactual/perturbation) designs over leaderboard maximization.

summary: Measuring capability: benchmarks beyond the loss curve.

title: Designing Evaluations
summary: Build evals that measure your claim — with baselines and error bars.

sections.beginner:
What: a good eval = task samples mirroring production + fixed protocol (shots, decoding, template) + baselines (base model, prior version, trivial heuristic) + held-out privacy.

Why: 'score went up' without baselines and protocol is noise with confidence. Baselines separate model progress from harness artifacts.

Example: support-bot eval: 300 real tickets (PII-scrubbed), greedy, your template, scored by rubric-judge calibrated on 50 human grades + exact-match on order IDs.
sections.intermediate:
How: stratify by difficulty/type (report slices, not just means); size for power (n ≈ 16·p(1−p)/δ² for margin δ — ~400 items for ±5% at p=0.5); screen train vs eval overlap; pin harness versions; average over 2–3 prompt templates.

Rule: a regression gate needs: metric, threshold, baseline, and seed protocol — 'looks better' is not a gate.
sections.advanced:
Implementation: LLM judges (rubric + few-shot + human agreement ≥ ~0.7 κ before trusting), pairwise arenas for open-ended quality, prospective/dated items (post-cutoff = contamination-proof), eval CI on every checkpoint promotion.

Failure modes: judge self-preference (same-family judge favors same-family models — cross-judge); length bias (longer wins lazy judges — normalize or penalize); saturated suites (all models 95%+ — retire or harden).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: scores estimate latent capability through noisy instruments: binomial sampling error, item-difficulty skew, prompt variance, judge error — total uncertainty is the sum, and most reported 'wins' sit inside it. Power analysis before data collection, confidence intervals on every claim, and pre-registered primary metrics are what separate measurement from leaderboard theater.

title: Perplexity & Loss

sections.beginner:
What: perplexity = exp(average cross-entropy loss). PPL 20 ≈ 'as confused as guessing among 20 tokens'. Lower is better, and it falls as training progresses.

Why: the cheapest health metric — computable on any text, no labels needed. Healthy run: train PPL falls smoothly; val PPL falls then flattens (stop near the flatten point).

Example: loss 3.0 → PPL 20.1; loss 2.0 → PPL 7.4; loss 1.0 → PPL 2.7. Random 7B start ≈ loss 11.7 → PPL ~120k (vocab-sized confusion).

Common mistake: comparing PPL across tokenizers/models with different vocabs — per-token units differ; compare same-tokenizer only.
sections.intermediate:
How: read curves: smooth joint fall = learning; train↓ val↑ = overfitting (stop/regularize/more data); both flat = underfit or LR too small; sudden spike = instability (check batch/LR/precision).

Rule: report train PPL, val PPL, and at least one downstream task — PPL alone never ships a decision.
sections.advanced: Implementation: domain-sliced PPL (code vs prose vs the target domain — aggregate PPL hides domain regressions); sliding-window PPL for long docs (avoid early-token cheap gains); bits-per-byte for cross-tokenizer comparison.
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: PPL = exp(H) where H is cross-entropy in nats — the effective branching factor. Its limits: it weights all tokens equally (a and the are as important as the key fact), rewards calibration over correctness, and correlates imperfectly with task success (a sharper wrong model can beat a humble right one on PPL while failing users). Hence: necessary, never sufficient.

summary: exp(loss): the cheapest health metric, and its limits.

title: FP32 Precision

sections.beginner:
What: FP32 (32-bit float): full range (~3.4e38), full precision, ~4 bytes/param. The safe default for accumulation, reductions, and optimizer states.

Why: every lower precision is a trade against this reference. When numerics confuse you, run the op in FP32 — if the problem vanishes, it was precision, not logic.

Example: 7B params in FP32 = 28 GB just for weights — why nobody trains pure FP32 anymore.
sections.intermediate: How: modern recipe keeps FP32 where it matters (master weights, Adam m/v, softmax/accumulation, loss scaling math) while compute/storage go BF16. Memory cost is why FP32-everything died: Adam FP32 full training ≈ 16 B/param before activations.
sections.advanced: Implementation: TF32 on Ampere+ (19-bit internal matmul with FP32 range — free speedup, toggle via backends, slight numeric difference vs pure FP32); keep reductions/norms in FP32 even in 'BF16' runs.
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: IEEE-754 FP32: 1 sign + 8 exponent + 23 mantissa bits; machine epsilon ~1.2e-7. LLM relevance: gradient updates (~1e-6 relative) need mantissa headroom the 16-bit formats lack — the fundamental reason master weights stay FP32 while matmuls go narrow.

summary: Full-precision reference for all numeric trade-offs.

title: FP16 Precision

sections.beginner:
What: FP16 (16-bit): half the memory of FP32 (2 bytes/param) but a narrow range — max only ~65,504. Big activations overflow to infinity.

Why it matters: FP16 was the first mixed-precision workhorse, but its range limit causes NaN/overflow in deep LLM training — the reason the field moved to BF16.

Example: attention logits or large FFN outputs exceeding 65k → inf → NaN loss. The classic FP16 training crash.

Common mistake: training LLMs in FP16 without loss scaling, then blaming the model for NaNs.
sections.intermediate:
How: loss scaling (multiply loss by 2^k before backward to keep small grads representable, unscale before the optimizer step); GradScaler automates it; overflow checks skip bad steps.

Rule: new training run? Use BF16, not FP16 — same memory, FP32-like range, no scaler babysitting. Reserve FP16 for inference or legacy GPUs without BF16 (T4/V100).
sections.advanced: Implementation: FP16 vs BF16 is an exponent/mantissa split (FP16: 5 exp + 10 mantissa; BF16: 8 exp + 7 mantissa) — FP16 is more precise in-range, BF16 is vastly wider. Training needs range (activations vary hugely); inference can prefer precision.
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: overflow probability grows with activation magnitude × depth — transformer residuals accumulate scales that routinely exceed 65k in large models, making FP16 overflow structural rather than accidental. Underflow matters too: subnormal grads flush to zero, silently killing small-but-real updates — loss scaling's raison d'être. Hardware note: pre-Ampere GPUs lack fast BF16, which is why FP16+scaling was mandatory history, not preference.

summary: Half precision with a narrow range: fast but overflow-prone.

title: BF16 (Bfloat16)

sections.beginner:
What: BF16 (bfloat16): 16 bits with FP32's range (~3.4e38) and reduced precision. Same 2 bytes/param as FP16, but activations essentially never overflow.

Why it behaves differently from FP16: range, not precision, is what training needs — BF16 keeps the 8-bit exponent (wide range) and sacrifices mantissa bits (precision). Overflow crashes disappear; tiny precision loss is harmless to optimization.

Example: the same run that NaNs in FP16 at step 200 trains cleanly in BF16 with zero other changes — the most common precision fix in LLM training.
sections.intermediate:
How: requirements: Ampere+ (A100/RTX30xx+) or newer, TPU, recent Apple Silicon. Recipe: autocast(dtype=bfloat16), usually no GradScaler, FP32 master weights + Adam states behind the scenes.

Rule: BF16 for training whenever hardware allows; FP16 only when hardware forces it (then add scaling + overflow vigilance).
sections.advanced: Implementation: BF16 matmul throughput equals FP16 on modern Tensor Cores; stochastic rounding (some HW) further closes the precision gap; keep embeddings/norms/loss in FP32 for free stability; verify actual dtype placement with the profiler (silent FP32 fallbacks waste the win).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: bit layout 1+8+7 vs FP16's 1+5+10: BF16 truncation of FP32 is literally dropping the low 16 bits — conversion is cheap and range-preserving. Rounding-error analysis: optimization tolerates relative error ~2^-8 fine (gradients are noisy anyway); what it cannot tolerate is inf/nan from overflow — hence range dominates precision for training stability. This single insight drove the industry FP16→BF16 migration.

summary: Brain float: FP32 range at half the memory. The training default.

title: Mixed Precision Training

sections.beginner:
What: mixed precision = BF16/FP16 for matmuls and storage, FP32 for master weights, optimizer states, and accumulation. Standard recipe: ~half the memory, ~1.5–2× the speed, same final quality.

Why: matmuls dominate cost and tolerate narrow types; reductions/updates need precision. Splitting by op type gets both wins.

Example: 7B full-FT, BF16-mixed with Adam: weights 14 GB + FP32 master 28 GB + grads 14 GB + states 56 GB ≈ 112 GB before activations — multi-GPU territory. Pure FP32 would be ~140 GB+. Mixed precision makes it possible, not small.

Common mistake: 'BF16 training uses 2 bytes/param' — only for weight storage; the full per-param training cost is ~16 bytes with Adam. Budget with the calculator, not the slogan.
sections.intermediate:
How: PyTorch AMP: autocast regions + (FP16 only) GradScaler; BF16 typically needs no scaler. Keep custom losses/norms in FP32; clip unscaled grads (the classic AMP bug is clipping scaled grads with an unscaled threshold).

Rule: default: BF16 autocast + FP32 master + AdamW + clip 1.0. Deviate with measurements, not hopes.
sections.advanced:
Implementation: op-level dtype placement (matmul/conv narrow; softmax/norm/loss wide); detecting silent FP32 fallbacks (profiler dtype view); FP8 training on Hopper (per-tensor/per-channel scaling, accumulator stays wide) — still experimental for pretraining, real for inference.

Failure modes: NaN in FP16 without scaler; scaler stuck tiny (chronic underflow — move to BF16); loss-scale desync after checkpoint resume (save scaler state).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: full per-param accounting (Adam, mixed BF16): 2 (weight) + 4 (FP32 master) + 2 (grad) + 4 (m) + 4 (v) = 16 B/param. Activations add batch·seq·hidden·layers·bytes (rough lower bound; FlashAttention lowers it). This is why 7B full-FT needs ~8×80 GB with margin while 7B QLoRA fits 8 GB: LoRA pays the 16 B rate on ~0.5% of params and ~0.5–0.6 B on the frozen rest (scales included).

summary: Narrow compute plus FP32 states: the standard recipe.

title: FP8 Precision

sections.beginner:
What: FP8 (8-bit float, 1 byte/param): E4M3 (more precision, range ±448) for weights/activations, E5M2 (more range) for gradients. Hopper (H100) and newer run it natively at ~2× BF16 throughput.

Why: halves weight memory vs BF16 and doubles matmul rate — the next step of the precision ladder for serving (and experimentally, training).

Example: 70B weights: 140 GB BF16 → 70 GB FP8 — the difference between 2×H100-80GB and squeezing onto fewer GPUs.

Common mistake: assuming any GPU runs FP8 — needs Hopper/Ada-generation or newer (or MI300X) + framework support; on older GPUs FP8 code silently falls back.
sections.intermediate:
How: inference: per-tensor or per-channel scaling (amax calibration on sample data); training: dynamic per-step scaling + FP16/BF16 master states; Transformer Engine automates format choice per layer.

Rule: FP8 for inference on supported HW after measuring quality delta on your evals; FP8 training stays experimental — budget debugging time.
sections.advanced: Implementation: cuBLAS FP8 paths, delayed-scaling recipe (track amax history, update scale every N steps), layers that must stay narrow-exempt (norms, softmax, loss); accumulation always ≥ FP16/BF16.
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: E4M3: 1+4+3 bits (max 448, fine steps); E5M2: 1+5+2 (max 57k, coarse). The dual-format design mirrors the BF16/FP16 lesson: forward needs precision, backward needs range. Scaling converts the representability problem into a statistics problem (track tensor amax, set scale = max_repr/amax × margin) — failures are stale-scale events, diagnosable from amax histories.

summary: 8-bit floats on Hopper and newer: 2x throughput, 1 byte per param.

title: Quantization

sections.beginner:
What: quantization stores weights in fewer bits: FP32 → FP16/BF16 → INT8 → INT4/NF4. 7B: 28 GB → 14 → 7 → ~4–5 GB effective at 4-bit (group scales and zero-points add ~10–30% over the raw 3.5 GB — 4-bit never means exactly 0.5 bytes/param). The question is always quality-per-byte.

Why: it decides what fits where: 70B BF16 needs 140 GB (multi-GPU); 70B 4-bit needs ~35 GB (one workstation GPU). Quantization is the difference between 'needs a cluster' and 'runs tonight'.

Example: LLaMA-3-8B: BF16 16 GB (needs 24 GB card with overhead) → INT8 ~8 GB → 4-bit ~4.5 GB (fits 8 GB cards via llama.cpp/GGUF).

Common mistake: quantizing to 4-bit then judging the base model — judge the quantized artifact on your evals; quality loss concentrates on math, code, and rare languages.
sections.intermediate:
How: PTQ (quantize after training — GPTQ/AWQ use calibration data to protect salient weights; GGUF for CPU/llama.cpp), QAT (train with quantization simulated — best quality, most effort), symmetric vs asymmetric (zero-point) ranges, group-wise (e.g., 128-weight groups share scales).

Rule: when is 4-bit good enough? Chat/summarization/RAG usually yes (verify!); precise math, code gen, and low-resource languages: test 8-bit/BF16 first — degradation concentrates there.

Trade-off: smaller groups + more calibration = better quality, slower quantization and slightly larger files.
sections.advanced:
Implementation: AWQ (protect top-1% salient weights by activation scale), GPTQ (Hessian-guided rounding), NF4 for QLoRA bases, KV-cache quantization (separate knob — 8-bit KV often free, 4-bit needs eval), serving unmerged LoRA on quantized bases.

Failure modes: calibration-set mismatch (quantize on English, serve multilingual — tail languages collapse); quantizing already-quantized artifacts (compounding error); throughput traps (some 4-bit kernels are memory-light but compute-slow on old GPUs).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: quantization error ≈ scale/√12 per weight (uniform) — outliers dominate, hence salient-weight protection and group-wise scales. Scaling laws for quantization: larger models quantize better (redundancy absorbs error — 70B@4-bit often beats 7B@8-bit at similar bytes). This is why 'which model at which bits' beats 'which bits' as the decision frame.

summary: Fewer bits per weight: what fits where, at what quality cost.

title: GPU Memory Anatomy

sections.beginner:
What: training memory has four tenants: weights, gradients, optimizer states, activations — plus framework overhead. Weights are the smallest part of training (unlike inference).

Why: CUDA OOM is the #1 training crash. Knowing which tenant overflows tells you the fix: activations → checkpointing/smaller batch; optimizer → LoRA/8-bit states; weights → quantization/sharding.

Example: 1B params, BF16, Adam, batch 4 × seq 2048: weights 2 GB + grads 2 + master 4 + states 8 = 16 GB before activations — already over a 12 GB card. This is why 1B full-FT wants 24 GB.

Common mistake: 'the model is 2 GB so it fits in 8 GB' — training costs ~8× weight storage with Adam. Use the VRAM calculator.
sections.intermediate:
How: per-param math (mixed BF16 + AdamW): weights 2 B + FP32 master 4 B + grads 2 B + Adam m/v 8 B = 16 B/param. Activations ≈ micro-batch × seq × hidden × layers × bytes (rough lower bound — attention backend and saved tensors shift it a lot; gradient-accumulation steps run sequentially and reuse the same buffers, so accumulation adds steps, not activation memory).

Rule: estimate, then keep 20% headroom: theoretical 19 GB on a 24 GB card is a maybe (fragmentation + CUDA context + spikes eat the rest).

Trade-off: bigger batch = better throughput per step but linear activation growth; grad accumulation buys batch size without activation growth (at slower wall-clock per step).
sections.advanced:
Implementation: fragmentation (reserved ≫ allocated in nvidia-smi — empty_cache helps rarely; lower fragmentation via stable shapes), CUDA context (~0.5–1 GB), NCCL buffers in distributed, dataloader worker RAM (CPU OOM is the quiet sibling).

Failure modes: OOM at step 0 (weights+optim don't fit — reduce model/precision/shard) vs OOM at step N (leak: growing graph, retained loss history — fix the code, not the batch).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: peak memory hits at different phases: forward peak (activations materialize), backward peak (grads + recompute overlap), optimizer peak (moment updates). Profiling per-phase with torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated + snapshots identifies the tenant — aggregate numbers cannot. Per-layer accounting: attention projections scale with h², FFN with 3·e·h², embeddings with vocab·h — the Model Calculator breaks this down.

summary: Where training memory goes: weights, grads, states, activations.

title: Memory Optimization Techniques

sections.beginner:
What: the big four memory savers: mixed precision (half the storage), gradient checkpointing (recompute activations — big savings, ~20–30% slower), smaller batch + grad accumulation (same math, less activation memory), LoRA/QLoRA (train 1% of params).

Why: combined they move 7B fine-tuning from '8×A100' to '1×RTX 4090' territory. Order matters: apply in the sequence that preserves quality (precision → checkpointing → batch → adapters).

Example: 7B SFT OOM at batch 8 → BF16 + checkpointing + batch 2 × accum 4 → fits, same effective batch, ~25% slower per step.
sections.intermediate:
How: activation checkpointing granularity (whole-block vs selective — attention-only checkpointing is often the sweet spot with FlashAttention); CPU offload (optimizer states, then weights — slow but huge); 8-bit Adam (halves state memory, verify convergence).

Rule: never cut batch size without adding grad accumulation to hold the effective batch constant — otherwise you changed the optimization, not just the memory.
sections.advanced:
Implementation: unified-memory tricks (Apple/AMD APUs — oversubscribe with paging at a bandwidth cost); paged attention for inference-side KV; framework flags (expandable_segments to fight fragmentation, SDPA backend selection).

Failure modes: offload thrashing (PCIe-bound step times 10× — profile before accepting); checkpoint-everything (recompute dominates — selective beats full).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: the memory–compute Pareto frontier: checkpointing converts O(L) activation storage to O(√L) with one extra forward (optimal segmenting); offloading converts VRAM to PCIe bandwidth (viable when arithmetic intensity is high); 8-bit states quantize m/v with error feedback. Frontier rule: pick the cheapest point that fits with 20% headroom — over-optimizing memory past fit just burns throughput.

summary: The big four memory savers, in quality-preserving order.

title: Gradient Checkpointing

sections.beginner:
What: normal training saves every layer's activations for the backward pass. Checkpointing saves only a few and recomputes the rest on demand — ~50–70% less activation memory for ~20–30% extra compute.

Why: activations (not weights) are usually what OOMs training at long context or big batch. Checkpointing directly attacks the biggest tenant.

Example: one line in HF Transformers: model.gradient_checkpointing_enable() — often the difference between batch 1 and batch 4.

Common mistake: enabling it and expecting identical step time — budget the recompute slowdown in run-time estimates.
sections.intermediate:
How: granularity: per-block (standard), selective (checkpoint attention, keep cheap ops — best with FlashAttention), full (max saving, max slowdown). Incompatible with some uses of torch.compile regions and in-place ops on recomputed tensors.

Rule: checkpoint the expensive-to-store, cheap-to-recompute ops (attention outputs, FFN intermediates); keep norms and small elementwise ops stored.
sections.advanced: Implementation: with FSDP: checkpoint before/after wrapping matters (wrap → checkpoint the FSDP-wrapped block to include all-gather in recompute correctly); with FlashAttention the attention map was never stored anyway — checkpoint the surrounding projections instead.
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: forward stores segment boundaries only; backward re-runs each segment then backprops through it. Optimal segmentation gives O(√L) memory for one extra forward pass total. Interaction with autograd: use_reentrant variants differ in RNG handling (dropout must replay identically — seed it or disable dropout under checkpointing).

summary: Recompute activations to trade compute for memory.

title: Data Parallelism (DDP)

sections.beginner:
What: Distributed Data Parallel: N GPUs each hold a full model copy, process different data shards, and average gradients (all-reduce) every step. The simplest multi-GPU training.

Why: near-linear speedup while the model fits on one GPU: 4 GPUs ≈ 3.5–3.8× the tokens/sec of one. First scaling step for every project.

Example: torchrun --nproc_per_node=4 train.py + DistributedDataParallel(model) + distributed sampler — 8 GPUs cut a 4-day run to ~13 hours.

Common mistake: forgetting the distributed sampler (every GPU sees the same data — 4× compute for 1× learning).
sections.intermediate:
How: broadcast weights at init, bucket all-reduce of grads overlapping backward compute, identical seeds + sampler epochs per rank. Effective batch = per-GPU batch × N (scale LR accordingly).

Rule: DDP requires the full model + grads + states on EACH GPU — if one GPU OOMs alone, DDP changes nothing. Shard (FSDP/ZeRO) instead.

Trade-off: communication per step ≈ 2× grad size ÷ bandwidth — small models on slow interconnect go communication-bound (adding GPUs slows steps).
sections.advanced: Implementation: uneven inputs (find_unused_parameters cost, static-graph mode), torch.compile + DDP ordering, gradient compression (PowerSGD/FP16 comms — verify convergence), multi-node rendezvous and elastic restarts.
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: ring all-reduce moves 2(N−1)/N × size bytes per rank — bandwidth-optimal and latency-tolerant. NCCL builds rings/trees over NVLink/IB automatically; PCIe-only topologies collapse to bus bandwidth (measure with nccl-tests before planning). Scaling efficiency = compute ÷ (compute + comm); it falls as model shrinks, batch shrinks, or network slows — the three knobs of every scaling postmortem.

summary: One model copy per GPU, averaged gradients: simplest multi-GPU.

title: Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP)

sections.beginner:
What: Fully Sharded Data Parallel shards the model's weights, grads, and optimizer states across GPUs — each GPU holds ~1/N of the total. 7B full-FT that needs 112 GB on one GPU needs ~16 GB/GPU on 8 GPUs.

Why: trains models that fit on no single GPU, with a DDP-like programming model. PyTorch's recommended path past single-GPU memory.

Example: wrap with FSDP(model, ...) under torchrun; per-step it all-gathers weights layer-by-layer (compute), then discards (memory stays sharded).

Common mistake: wrapping without a sharding strategy for uneven layers (embeddings/lm_head dominate — shard or CPU-offload them explicitly).
sections.intermediate:
How: ZeRO stages via FSDP: stage 1 (shard optimizer), 2 (+ grads), 3 (+ weights — full FSDP). FSDP2 (per-param sharding) + torch.compile is the current stack. Backward prefetch overlaps comms; CPU offload extends to bigger models at PCIe cost.

Rule: start FULL_SHARD (stage 3) + auto wrapping by block; drop to HYBRID_SHARD across slow inter-node links (shard within node, replicate across).
sections.advanced:
Implementation: checkpoint save/load across world sizes (sharded ↔ consolidated formats); mixing with gradient checkpointing (order: checkpoint → wrap); uneven-param layers and limit_all_gathers tuning; FSDP2 + DTensor for composability with TP.

Failure modes: version-skewed checkpoint loads; all-gather storms from too-fine wrapping (wrap per transformer block, not per linear); CPU-offload thrash misdiagnosed as slow GPUs.
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: per-step traffic ≈ 3× params (all-gather forward + all-gather backward + reduce-scatter grads) vs DDP's ~2× grads — FSDP trades extra communication for ÷N memory. Overlap (prefetch) hides most of it when compute ≥ comms; the crossover is why FSDP shines on big models/fast networks and underwhelms on small models/slow links. Eager vs lazy init changes peak build memory — init on meta device for 70B+ builds.

summary: Sharded data parallel: train models bigger than one GPU.

title: DeepSpeed ZeRO

sections.beginner:
What: ZeRO (Zero Redundancy Optimizer, DeepSpeed) is the sharding idea FSDP implements: stage 1 shards optimizer states, stage 2 adds gradients, stage 3 adds weights — each stage roughly divides that tenant's memory by N.

Why: same math as FSDP, different ecosystem (DeepSpeed adds Infinity offload to CPU/NVMe, sparse attention kernels, and one-click configs). Choose by stack, not by theory.

Example: 7B + ZeRO-3 on 4×A100-40GB: ~112 GB total ÷ 4 ≈ 28 GB/GPU + activations — fits where DDP (112 GB/GPU) cannot start.
sections.intermediate:
How: DeepSpeed config JSON (zero_optimization.stage 1/2/3, offload flags, overlap_comm); stage choice = smallest stage that fits (stage 1–2 keep full weights for simplicity when possible); ZeRO-Infinity pushes to CPU/NVMe for 100B+ on modest clusters.

Rule: PyTorch-native project → FSDP2; need NVMe offload / DeepSpeed kernels / established ZeRO recipes → DeepSpeed. Don't mix both.
sections.advanced: Implementation: offload tuning (which tensors, prefetch depth), overlap settings per interconnect, ZeRO-3 + checkpointing + CPU-offload combined recipes for 70B on 8×40 GB; comparing measured step times, not just fit — stage 3's extra comms cost real throughput.
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: stage 3 communication ≈ 3× params/step (gather×2 + scatter) with memory ≈ params/N + working buffers; partitioning analysis shows stage 2 is often the efficiency sweet spot (weights replicated, everything else sharded) when the model barely exceeds one GPU. Offload economics: NVMe bandwidth (~3–7 GB/s) vs HBM (~2–3 TB/s) — three orders of magnitude, viable only because offloaded tensors (optimizer states) are touched once per step, not per op.

summary: DeepSpeed sharding stages 1-3 plus CPU/NVMe offload.

title: Tensor Parallelism

sections.beginner:
What: tensor parallelism splits individual layers across GPUs: GPU 0 computes half of every matmul, GPU 1 the other half, combining results each layer. For when the model is too wide for one GPU.

Why: data-parallel methods still need each GPU to materialize full layers during compute; TP never does. 70B inference on 2×24 GB cards is a TP workload.

Example: attention heads split 64 → 32+32; FFN rows split; each layer boundary does one all-reduce to rejoin.

Common mistake: TP across PCIe-only GPUs — per-layer syncs on slow links make it slower than fewer GPUs.
sections.intermediate:
How: column-parallel then row-parallel splits (one sync per block); kv_heads and head counts must divide by TP degree; Megatron-style layouts in vLLM/TGI via tensor_parallel_size.

Rule: TP group = GPUs inside one NVLink domain (typically ≤8); across nodes use data/pipeline parallelism instead.
sections.advanced: Implementation: vLLM PagedAttention + TP (KV sharded consistently with heads); sequence-parallel add-ons for norm/dropout; TP + FSDP/DP hybrids (2D parallelism) for 70B+ training.
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: TP communication per layer ≈ 2 all-reduces of activation size (batch·seq·hidden) — bandwidth ∝ activations, unlike DP's ∝ params. Hence the decision rule: TP wins when params ≫ activations per step (wide models, small batches — i.e., inference); DP wins when activations dominate (training with big batches). Bandwidth requirement ≈ activation bytes × layers ÷ step-time budget — NVLink-class (~300–900 GB/s) vs PCIe (~32–64 GB/s) decides feasibility.

summary: Splitting layers across GPUs for wide models.

title: Pipeline Parallelism

sections.beginner:
What: pipeline parallelism splits the model by layers: GPU 0 runs layers 0–7, GPU 1 runs 8–15, etc. Micro-batches flow through like an assembly line.

Why: for very deep models where even sharded single layers fit but the whole model doesn't — or to combine with TP (TP within node, pipeline across nodes).

Example: 80-layer 70B across 8 GPUs = 10 layers each; 32 micro-batches keep the pipe mostly full.

Common mistake: too few micro-batches (GPUs idle = 'bubble') or uneven layer splits (one slow stage gates everything).
sections.intermediate:
How: micro-batch count ≥ 4× pipeline stages to hide the bubble; interleaved schedules (each GPU handles multiple non-adjacent chunks) shrink bubble further; balance by measured layer time, not layer count (early/late layers differ).

Rule: bubble fraction ≈ (stages−1) ÷ micro-batches — size micro-batches from this, not from habit.

Trade-off: more stages = less memory/GPU but more bubble + more point-to-point comms; activation stashing grows with in-flight micro-batches.
sections.advanced: Implementation: 2D/3D layouts (DP × TP × PP) for 400B+; ZeRO-style sharding inside pipeline stages; async P2P to overlap stage transfers; fault tolerance per stage (a dead stage kills the pipe — checkpoint accordingly).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: optimal schedules (1F1B, interleaved 1F1B) minimize bubble to ~(p−1)/(m) with memory O(m/p) trade-offs; pipeline + TP interaction: TP reduces per-layer time (smaller bubble penalty) while PP reduces per-GPU memory — the 3D design point balances comms volume (TP, bandwidth-hungry) against latency exposure (PP, bubble). Ring vs mesh P2P topologies matter past ~16 stages.

summary: Splitting by layers with micro-batched assembly lines.

title: Expert Parallelism

sections.beginner:
What: for Mixture-of-Experts models: each GPU hosts a few experts; tokens travel the network to their assigned experts and back. Data-parallelism's analog for sparse models.

Why: MoE total params (e.g., 47B) exceed any one GPU while active params (13B) don't — expert parallelism stores the inactive experts elsewhere.

Example: Mixtral 8×7B on 4 GPUs: 2 experts each; every token's router picks 2 experts, possibly on other GPUs.
sections.intermediate:
How: expert placement (balance hot experts), all-to-all dispatch/combine collectives, capacity factors (drop overflow tokens past capacity — quality knob), load-balance auxiliary loss during training.

Rule: all-to-all bandwidth is the MoE scaling ceiling — measure it (nccl-tests alltoall) before committing to big expert counts.
sections.advanced: Implementation: DeepSpeed-MoE / Megatron-MoE stacks; expert + tensor hybrid (TP inside experts, EP across); dropless routing (no token drop, variable latency) vs capped (bounded latency, some drop).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: MoE comms per layer ≈ 2 all-to-alls of (tokens × top-k × hidden) — grows with batch × k, not with expert count, which is why MoE scales params nearly free but not batch. Load imbalance (popular experts) creates stragglers; auxiliary losses and shared-expert designs (DeepSeek-style) smooth it. At scale, EP network behavior dominates step time — profile all-to-all, not matmuls.

summary: Placing MoE experts on different GPUs.

title: Mixture of Experts (MoE)

sections.beginner:
What: Mixture of Experts replaces each FFN with E parallel FFNs ('experts') + a router sending each token to the top-k (usually 2). 47B total params, ~13B active per token (Mixtral 8×7B).

Why: scale params (knowledge capacity) without scaling FLOPs per token (cost). The only architecture that has scaled past dense limits economically.

Example: token 'photosynthesis' routes to biology-ish experts; 'eigenvalue' to math-ish ones — specialization emerges, it is not assigned.

Common mistake: judging MoE by total params ('47B model') — compare active params and measured quality; total params measure memory, not smarts-per-token.
sections.intermediate:
How: top-k routing (k=1 Switch, k=2 standard), load-balance loss (penalize collapsing onto one expert), expert capacity (max tokens per expert per step), shared experts (always-on generalist + routed specialists).

Rule: fine-tuning MoE: tune the router gently (low LR) or freeze it early — router collapse (all tokens → 2 experts) is the characteristic failure.

Trade-off: sparse quality-per-FLOP wins vs dense complexity (routing, imbalance, all-to-all serving infra, fine-tuning brittleness).
sections.advanced: Implementation: Switch/GShard/Shazeer lineage; DeepSeek-style fine-grained experts + shared experts (current SOTA recipe); upcycling (dense → MoE conversion + continued training); MoE + quantization (experts quantize well — redundancy again).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: routing is learned discrete assignment — non-differentiable, trained via straight-through/load-balance proxies; expert collapse and representation collapse are distinct failure attractors. Research frontier: learned k, hierarchical routing, expert-choice (experts pick tokens — perfect balance, variable coverage). Production note: MoE inference needs expert-parallel serving or full replication — memory planning uses total params, latency planning uses active.

summary: Sparse expert models: scale params without scaling FLOPs.

title: Inference Basics

sections.beginner:
What: inference = autoregressive generation: feed prompt → predict token → append → repeat. Two phases: prefill (process the prompt, compute-bound) and decode (emit one token at a time, memory-bandwidth-bound).

Why: the phases have opposite bottlenecks — prefill wants FLOPs, decode wants memory bandwidth. Every serving optimization targets one of them.

Example: 70B on 2×A100: prefill 2000 tokens in ~2 s, then ~30 tokens/s decode. Long prompt? Prefill dominates. Chatbot? Decode dominates.

Common mistake: benchmarking only prefill speed for a chatbot workload (or vice versa).
sections.intermediate:
How: KV cache (store past K/V — decode becomes O(1)-per-token work with O(n) state), batching (share weight reads across requests), quantization (shrink weights → faster decode, which is bandwidth-bound).

Rule: decode throughput ≈ memory_bandwidth ÷ bytes_per_token_step — estimate any serving setup from this before benchmarking.
sections.advanced: Implementation: continuous batching (insert new requests mid-generation), speculative decoding (draft model proposes, big model verifies — 2–3× faster when acceptance is high), chunked prefill (don't stall decodes behind huge prompts).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: roofline view: prefill sits in the compute-bound region (arithmetic intensity high), decode in the memory-bound region (each step streams all weights for ~2·params FLOPs). vLLM/PagedAttention attack decode memory fragmentation; TensorRT-LLM/SGLang fuse the decode path into bandwidth-optimal kernels. Latency vs throughput is a batch-size walk along this roofline.

summary: Prefill vs decode: the two phases of generation.

title: KV Cache

sections.beginner:
What: without caching, generating token 1000 would recompute attention over all 999 previous tokens from scratch. KV cache stores their Keys and Values once — each new token only computes its own Q/K/V and attends to the cache.

Why it grows with context: every token adds one K vector + one V vector per layer per KV head. Longer context = more cached vectors, linearly: double the context, double the cache.

Example: LLaMA-3-8B BF16: 2 × 32 layers × 8 KV heads × 128 dim × 2 bytes = 131 KB per token. 8k context ≈ 1 GB; 128k ≈ 16 GB — per request.

Common mistake: sizing inference by weights only ('8B = 16 GB, fits 24 GB') then OOMing on the first long-context batch.
sections.intermediate:
How: formula: 2 × seq × layers × kv_heads × head_dim × bytes × batch. Why GQA reduces it: fewer KV heads = proportionally fewer cached vectors (32→8 heads = 4× smaller). KV precision (FP8/INT8 KV) is a separate knob from weight precision.

Rule: budget weights + (cache per request × max concurrent requests) + ~1–2 GB runtime. Use the Inference Memory calculator for your numbers.

Trade-off: longer context or bigger batch — pick one per GB; serving systems trade them continuously.
sections.advanced:
Implementation: PagedAttention (vLLM: non-contiguous block allocation — kills fragmentation, enables big batches), prefix caching (share system-prompt cache across requests), sliding-window (Mistral: cache only last W tokens), eviction policies (StreamingLLM keeps attention sinks + recent).

Failure modes: fragmentation OOM with naive contiguous allocators (looks like a leak — switch to paged); evicting attention sinks (quality cliff — always pin early tokens).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: cache bytes scale as O(L·h_kv·d·n) — linear in every factor, which is why GQA (h_kv), quantization (bytes), and windowed attention (effective n) multiply. Quantized-KV analysis: K tolerates coarser quantization than V unevenly across heads (outlier channels) — per-channel K + per-token V schemes dominate. Fundamental limit: full-attention generation is Ω(n) state per request — sub-quadratic serving requires changing attention itself (linear/SSM hybrids, sparse patterns).

summary: Cached keys and values: why context costs memory linearly.

title: Inference Batching
summary: Latency vs throughput — and the batching that serves both.

sections.beginner:
What: batching shares one weight read across many requests (decode is bandwidth-bound, so sharing = free throughput). Static batching waits for full groups; continuous batching swaps finished requests for new ones mid-generation (the vLLM default).

Why: batch 32 rarely costs 32× the latency of batch 1 in decode — often ~2–5× when KV traffic still fits bandwidth — so throughput per GPU multiplies while p50 latency barely moves. p99 needs admission control, and past the KV/bandwidth ceiling batching stops helping.

Example: chatbot at 20 tok/s single → batched 16 concurrent ≈ 200+ tok/s aggregate, per-user latency +30%.
sections.intermediate:
How: size max batch from KV budget (cache/request × concurrency + weights + headroom); chunked prefill (split huge prompts so decodes don't stall); prefix caching (shared system prompts computed once); priority/preemption policies for SLO tiers.

Rule: cap concurrency by measured KV pressure, not by hope — overflow past the cache budget collapses everything (recompute storms).
sections.advanced: Implementation: disaggregated prefill/decode (separate GPUs per phase at scale); speculative decoding alongside batching (acceptance drops under heavy batch — measure jointly); queueing theory for SLOs (utilization >70% without control = p99 explosion).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: decode step time ≈ weights_bytes ÷ bandwidth (batch-independent until KV traffic competes) + KV_bytes(batch) ÷ bandwidth — the linear term sets the batch ceiling. Continuous batching is shortest-remaining-time-ish scheduling over an iterable process; iteration-level (vs request-level) scheduling is what unlocks the utilization win. Model it as a queue with service rate μ(batch) and size buffers for burst headroom, not averages.

title: Text Sampling Strategies

sections.beginner:
What: sampling turns token probabilities into actual text: greedy (always top-1 — deterministic), temperature (reshape sharp↔flat), top-k (keep best K), top-p/nucleus (keep the smallest set covering p of mass).

Why: the same model writes a precise API call (greedy, temp 0) or a varied story (temp 0.8, top-p 0.95) purely by decoding settings. Half of 'model quality' complaints are sampling misconfiguration.

Example: factual QA: temp 0–0.2, top-p 1. Brainstorming: temp 0.7–0.9, top-p 0.9–0.95. Code: temp 0–0.2 (correctness over variety).

Common mistake: cranking temperature to fix a weak prompt — randomness is not reasoning; fix the prompt/model first.
sections.intermediate:
How: repetition/presence/frequency penalties (suppress loops and regurgitation), min-p (adaptive floor — cleaner than top-k across distributions), combining (temp + top-p + penalties is the standard stack; avoid temp + top-k + top-p all aggressive at once).

Rule: evals use greedy (comparability); users get tuned sampling (experience). Never compare models with different decoding settings.
sections.advanced: Implementation: constrained generation (grammars/JSON schemas —833× fewer parse failures for structured output), contrastive/speculative-assisted decoding, guided decoding for tool calls (logit bias on syntax tokens).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: temperature T divides logits: p ∝ exp(z/T) — T→0 is argmax, T→∞ is uniform; entropy grows monotonically in T. Nucleus sampling adapts the candidate set to distribution shape (flat distributions keep many, peaked keep few) — the theoretical edge over fixed top-k. Repetition loops are attractor states of greedy decoding on peaked distributions; penalties reshape the landscape per-step. No universal recipe exists because the optimal point depends on the task's tolerance for variance — calibrate per task.

summary: Greedy, temperature, top-k, top-p: turning probabilities into text.

title: Throughput & MFU

sections.beginner:
What: throughput = tokens/second (per GPU for training; per system with latency percentiles for serving). MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) = achieved ÷ peak FLOPs — how much of the GPU you actually use.

Why: MFU turns 'slow' into a number: 45% MFU training is healthy; 8% means something is very wrong (usually data loading or tiny batches). 'Why can a model fit but train slowly?' — fit is memory, speed is utilization; small batches and CPU bottlenecks starve the GPU.

Example: 7B BF16 on H100 (989 BF16 TFLOPS dense): 45% MFU ≈ 445 TFLOPS ≈ ~10k tokens/s/GPU (at 6·N FLOP/token ≈ 42 GFLOP/token).

Common mistake: quoting nvidia-smi 'GPU-Util' as efficiency — 100% 'util' with tiny kernels = busy-waiting, not throughput. Measure tokens/s and MFU.
sections.intermediate:
How: measure: theoretical FLOP/token (6·N training, 2·N inference) → achieved = tokens/s × FLOP/token → MFU = achieved ÷ peak. Breakdown step time (forward/backward/optim/comm/dataloader) to find the bottleneck tenant.

Rule: targets: pretraining MFU 40–60% (well-tuned), SFT 30–50%, below 20% = stop and profile (dataloader workers, batch size, comm overlap, kernel backends).
sections.advanced:
Implementation: raising MFU: bigger micro-batches (memory permitting), FlashAttention/SDPA backends, torch.compile, comm-compute overlap (DDP buckets, FSDP prefetch), dataloader workers + pinned memory + compiled tokenization.

Failure modes: samples/sec vs tokens/sec confusion (packing changes the ratio); MFU gaming via counting recompute FLOPs (report both with/without checkpointing).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: peak FLOPS is a dense-matmul fantasy — real workloads mix memory-bound ops (norms, softmax, elementwise: intensity ~1 FLOP/byte) with compute-bound matmuls. Roofline: achievable = min(peak, bandwidth × intensity). MFU ceilings follow from the op mix (~60–70% for transformer training); the gap to peak is memory traffic, kernel-launch overhead, and collectives — profile-guided, not hype-guided, optimization closes it.

summary: Tokens per second and MFU: measuring real efficiency.

title: Profiling & Debugging

sections.beginner:
What: profiling measures where time and memory actually go: step-time split (data/forward/backward/optim), GPU util vs throughput, per-op CUDA time, memory timeline.

Why: every slowdown guess ('need more GPUs') is wrong until profiled — most are dataloaders, tiny batches, or a CPU bottleneck. Profile before spending.

Example: torch.profiler + TensorBoard: one glance shows dataloader at 60% of step time → raise num_workers, problem solved in minutes.

Common mistake: optimizing the model before the pipeline — data starvation is the most common 'slow GPU' cause.
sections.intermediate:
How: torch.profiler (CPU+CUDA table sorted by cuda_time_total), nvidia-smi dmon (live util/mem/power), wandb/TensorBoard (loss + throughput + memory trends), CUDA event timers for manual regions, flame graphs for CPU-side hotspots.

Rule: classify first: GPU-bound (kernels saturated → bigger batch/compile/flash) vs CPU-bound (gaps between kernels → workers/pinning/preprocessing) vs comm-bound (distributed overlap).
sections.advanced:
Implementation: Nsight Systems for timeline truth (kernel gaps, NCCL stalls, memcpy storms), NCCL_DEBUG + nccl-tests for fabric issues, memory snapshots (torch.cuda.memory_snapshot) for fragmentation forensics, multi-node aligned traces.

Failure modes: profiler overhead distorting short steps (profile steady-state, warm up first); tracing without CUDA sync (misattributed times); single-rank traces hiding stragglers (trace all ranks, compare).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: systematic method: establish roofline expectation → measure achieved → attribute the gap top-down (step → phase → op → kernel) with traces at each level. Straggler analysis (max vs p50 rank time) separates systemic from skew problems. At scale, 1% per-step overhead (logging, sync, checkpoint polling) compounds to days — the profiler's real job is finding the boring 1%s.

summary: Finding the actual bottleneck before spending money.

title: Reproducibility & Experiment Tracking
summary: Make every run attributable and re-runnable.

sections.beginner:
What: record per run: code hash, config, data version, env (CUDA/driver/lib pins), seed, and the resulting metrics + checkpoint. No record = no result.

Why: 'best LR 2e-4' is meaningless without the batch, data mix, and seed it came with. Untracked wins don't compound.

Example: one wandb/TensorBoard run per training with config + git hash + data manifest hash logged at step 0.
sections.intermediate:
How: seed Python/random/numpy/torch (+ CUDA deterministic flags for debugging — slower, use for diagnosis not production); deterministic data order (seeded shuffle, resumable offsets); config-as-code (no CLI-only runs).

Rule: expect run-to-run variance (±1–2% eval noise is normal) — compare seed-averaged or accept overlapping error bars, not single lucky runs.
sections.advanced: Implementation: full determinism is impossible across GPU types/counts (different reduction orders) — reproduce distributions, not bits; track hardware topology with results; nondeterminism-bisect protocol (CPU → single-GPU-det → multi-GPU) for stochastic bugs.
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: nondeterminism sources: parallel reduction order (atomics), autotuned kernels (benchmark mode picks per-shape winners), async dataloaders, NCCL collectives. Deterministic flags trade 10–30% throughput for bitwise repeatability on fixed topology — the right tool for debugging, the wrong default for training. Report variance, not just means: seed-sensitivity is itself a finding about landscape sharpness.

title: Deployment Basics

sections.beginner:
What: deployment = model file → running service: load weights into an inference engine (vLLM, TGI, llama.cpp, TensorRT-LLM), expose an API, watch it. Path: local script → workstation → server → container → production API.

Why: a model that only runs in a notebook helps one person once. Deployment multiplies every quality win by every request — and every bug too.

Example: 8B BF16 + vLLM on one 24 GB GPU: OpenAI-compatible endpoint in ~10 lines of config, ~30–60 tok/s.

Common mistake: serving the training checkpoint format directly (safe-serialize, quantize for the target GPU, pin engine + model versions together).
sections.intermediate:
How: containerize (CUDA base + pinned deps + model snapshot), concurrency via continuous batching (not one-process-per-request), health checks (ready/live + a smoke generation), versioning (model artefacts immutable, tagged, rollback-ready), basic autoscaling on queue depth.

Rule: load-test before launch: concurrent clients × your p95 prompt/completion mix → required GPUs = ceil(peak_load ÷ measured_per-GPU_throughput) + 1 spare.
sections.advanced:
Implementation: multi-model serving (shared base + LoRA adapters per tenant), canary/A-B rollouts with eval-gated promotion, observability (tokens/s, TTFT, ITL, queue time, KV pressure, error classes), failure handling (queue overflow → shed with 429, GPU crash → drain + reschedule), security basics (auth, rate limits, prompt-injection logging, PII redaction in logs).

Failure modes: KV-pressure collapse under bursty long prompts (admission control by estimated KV bytes); cold-start latency (prewarm + cached engines); silent quality drift after re-quantization (gate deploys on evals).
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: serving economics: cost/token ≈ GPU-hour ÷ tokens/hour at target latency — quantization and batching move this 5–20×, dwarfing GPU-price shopping. Latency decomposition (TTFT = queue + prefill; ITL = decode step) tells you which knob to turn. Capacity planning uses the Lindley queue lens: utilization >~70% without admission control = latency explosion under bursts — provision headroom, not averages.

summary: From checkpoint to production API.

title: Serving Observability & Ops
summary: Metrics, health, versioning, and rollback for LLM services.

sections.beginner:
What: observe four layers: service (uptime, 5xx, latency TTFT/ITL), pipeline (queue depth, KV pressure, batch size), quality (sampled outputs vs rubric, refusal/safety rates), cost (tokens/s/GPU, $/1k tokens).

Why: LLMs fail softly (worse answers, same 200 OK) — uptime dashboards miss quality regressions that cost users. Sample and score production traffic.

Example: alert on: p99 TTFT > SLO, KV pressure >85%, judge-scored sample quality drop >5 pts week-over-week.
sections.intermediate:
How: health endpoints (live vs ready vs a smoke generation), structured logs (prompt hash + config + timings, never raw PII), dashboards per layer, canary deploys gated on evals + live-sample comparison.

Rule: every model artefact immutable + tagged; rollback = one config flip, practicable at 3 AM (drill it).
sections.advanced: Implementation: multi-adapter serving ops (per-tenant LoRA routing + quotas), A/B with sticky bucketing, incident runbooks (KV-pressure shed → 429 + autoscale; crash loop → drain + pin last-good), red-team + injection-attempt logging.
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: treat serving as queueing + economics: Little's-law capacity from measured service rates, SLO-constrained autoscaling on queue depth (not CPU), cost attribution per tenant via token accounting. Quality observability is statistical process control on sampled scores — control limits, not vibes, trigger rollbacks.

title: Dataset Systems in Production
summary: How production dataset systems work: staged pipelines, manifests, gates, and calibration.

sections.beginner:
What: a dataset system turns a pile of raw files into versioned, trustworthy training data through fixed stages: collect, clean, dedupe, score, human spot-check, then release with a manifest. Each stage reads only the previous stage output and writes a new directory. Raw inputs are never modified.

Why: datasets outlive models - the same corpus trains this year's 8B and next year's replacement. Without stages plus manifests, 'the data we trained on' is unanswerable: silent corruption, duplicated records overweighting some topics, train/eval leakage discovered after the run.

Example: 10,000 scraped posts: exact-dedup drops 1,200 byte-identical copies, a heuristic scorer flags 800 low-quality records, a 200-item human spot-check measures the scorer at 85% agreement, and release v0.1 records input hashes, code version, and keep/drop counts in its manifest.

Common mistake: versioning by folder names (v1_final). Real versioning is a manifest with content hashes: any byte change anywhere produces a different hash, so versions are checkable instead of trustable-by-name.
sections.intermediate:
How: stage contracts (declared inputs, outputs, and determinism: same inputs plus same code version gives same outputs - record the code hash in the manifest); manifests (per-release record of version, parent hash, per-artifact SHA-256, counts, gate results); gates (boolean checks with thresholds: minimum quality score, maximum dup rate, license allowlist, eval overlap of zero); calibration (stratified sample across categories and sources, humans grade it, compare against the auto-scorer for accuracy overall plus bias per slice, then recalibrate or tighten gates).

Rule: no stage mutates upstream data; every release must be reproducible from manifest plus code hash plus raw inputs.

Trade-off: strict gates slow ingestion (human review is the bottleneck) while loose gates compound garbage - size review samples to risk: spot checks for routine intake, full review for releases.
sections.advanced:
Implementation: hash chaining (each manifest embeds the previous manifest hash, giving tamper-evident history); content addressing (artifacts identified by SHA-256, dedup by content not filename); near-dedup (MinHash/LSH Jaccard estimation catches paraphrase-level dupes that exact hashing misses); canonical records plus views (one model-agnostic JSONL source of truth with per-template converters versioned separately, so adding a model never migrates data); eval hygiene (generate splits with n-gram overlap checks against benchmarks at release time, not as an afterthought).

Failure modes: gate theater (thresholds everything passes - a gate that rejects nothing measures nothing); stale cards (docs describing v0.1 while v1.0 ships); exact-only dedup sold as dedup; calibration drift (scorer validated on an old distribution while data shifted); converter sprawl (hand-edited per-model files instead of generated views).

Reference implementation: the Atlas dataset system runs this architecture end to end (staged pipeline, hash-chained manifests, calibrated quality engine, approval-gated releases) - see the Source Library.
sections.deepdive: Mechanics: a content hash is an identity: SHA-256 collision resistance makes accidental collision negligible, so verification is recompute-and-compare. Chain verification walks parent hashes back to genesis. Stratified sampling allocates review budget across categories and sources to bound per-slice error, not just global accuracy. MinHash with k permutations estimates Jaccard similarity with standard error around 1/sqrt(k): k=128 gives roughly plus-or-minus 9% per pair, fine for ranking candidates with exact confirmation on the shortlist. Canonical-plus-views is single-source-of-truth applied to data: N model formats generated deterministically from one canonical form means fixes propagate by regeneration.
